title: Random-Sign IBLTs: Calibration-Free Self-Sizing After Decoding Failure

paper.title: Random-Sign IBLTs: Calibration-Free Self-Sizing After Decoding Failure
paper.abstract: Abstract In a two-round set reconciliation protocol based on an Invertible Bloom Lookup Table (IBLT), the first round sends a fixed-capacity table. If an oversized difference causes decoding failure, the receiver must estimate a safe upper bound on the unknown difference size d d from the sum of squared counts in the difference table to size the second-round table adaptively. The standard IBLT uses each element’s set direction as its accumulation sign. This couples the hypergraph-overlap bias induced by failure selection with the sign composition of the two-sided difference. A one-sided difference amplifies the estimation bias through contributions of the same sign, forcing existing schemes to rely on extensive offline simulation calibration over a grid of configurations. We propose the random-sign IBLT . A pseudorandom sign independent of the position mapping decouples failure selection from sign composition while preserving the number and width of cell fields and the peeling recovery capability. We prove that the estimator is exactly unbiased on every fixed failed hypergraph. For large differences, we prove a Gaussian limit for the estimation error conditioned on failure and derive a closed-form Gaussian upper bound. For small differences, we characterize a discrete limit distribution dominated by duplicate edge pairs and construct a Skellam upper-bound rule whose conditional miss rate is asymptotically at most the target risk, uniformly over all d ≥ 2 d\geq 2 without offline calibration. Five hundred million paired trials and end-to-end experiments with the real protocol spanning several orders of magnitude in load show that the random-sign IBLT eliminates direction sensitivity. For small differences, the conditional miss rate of the Gaussian upper bound exceeds the target by more than a factor of 8, whereas the Skellam upper-bound rule keeps it at or below the target level within sampling error across all 189 load configurations. The total two-round communication cost approaches that of an oracle using the true difference size in the same protocol.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Many distributed systems require two network endpoints holding sets A A and B B to find their symmetric difference A ​ △ ​ B A\triangle B , the elements present on only one side. This problem is called set reconciliation. The Invertible Bloom Lookup Table (IBLT) [ 17 , 13 ] is the standard data structure for this task. Each side builds a table of M M cells and hashes each element into the count, keySum, and checksum fields of k k cells. The receiver then subtracts the tables cell by cell. Shared elements contribute identical values to the same cells and cancel exactly, leaving only the contributions of the d = | A ​ △ ​ B | d=|A\triangle B| differing elements. An element present only in A A has direction + 1 +1 , and an element present only in B B has direction − 1 -1 . When the difference size d d is small enough relative to the table size M M (the load d / M d/M is below the peeling threshold), the receiver repeatedly finds a pure cell containing a single differing element and recovers all differing elements through peeling. Once d d exceeds the table’s capacity, peeling stalls and decoding fails. An IBLT presents a basic tension: the table size M M must be fixed at construction, yet the difference size d d remains unknown until synchronization completes. In practice, d d for the same pair of nodes can vary by several orders of magnitude over time. During routine synchronization, the two sides are nearly identical and d d is small. After recovery from a network partition or a batch write, d d can grow sharply. Allocating a large table for the worst case wastes bandwidth in most routine synchronizations. Allocating a small table causes decoding failure when the difference is large. The two-round protocol [ 32 ] addresses this tension. The first round sends a small table of fixed size, allowing routine small differences to complete in one round. If an oversized difference causes decoding failure, the count array of the difference table still retains the superimposed contributions of all d d differing elements. The receiver estimates an upper bound U U on d d from the sum of squared counts in this table. The second round allocates sufficient capacity based on U U and completes synchronization. The key requirement is to control the underestimate risk conditioned on failure (the conditional miss rate). If U < d U<d (a miss), insufficient capacity puts the second-round table at risk of another failure. An overly conservative U U wastes second-round bandwidth. The method in [ 32 ] uses the count sum and the sum of squared counts in the first-round difference table to construct an unbiased estimator d ^ \widehat{d} and obtain an upper bound U U by inversion. Estimating d d after failure is difficult because decoding failure itself selects the sample, and this selection couples with the sign composition of the set difference (the ratio of differing elements from A A to those from B B ). When we estimate d d with this sum-of-squares method, each element’s own contribution is fixed. The estimation error comes entirely from cross terms between differing elements that fall into the same cell. The standard IBLT uses each element’s set-membership direction ( + 1 +1 or − 1 -1 ) as its accumulation sign in count. Two elements with the same direction add when they share a cell, increasing the sum of squares. Elements with opposite directions cancel. Peeling success depends on how the position mappings of differing elements to cells overlap. Conditioning on failure therefore changes the overlap distribution. Together, these effects produce systematic bias in the failure sample. For a one-sided difference, all differing elements come from the same side. This is common in one-way synchronization, for example when a replica lacks only data newly written to the primary. All cross terms then have the same sign, so the change in overlap induced by failure is amplified in the sum of squared counts, substantially biasing the estimate. In two-way synchronization where each side writes new data, the numbers of differing elements on the two sides are comparable. For this balanced difference, positive and negative cross terms largely cancel, leaving the post-failure mean estimate nearly unchanged. The bias magnitude varies continuously with the ratio of differing elements on the two sides, and its sign reverses with the number of hashes k k (Section 2 ). After decoding failure, the receiver does not know whether the difference comes from one side or both. The observed sum of squared counts therefore cannot reveal how much is due to the true d d and how much to the direction bias induced by failure selection. Thus, except in deep overload, the upper-bound rule for the standard IBLT in [ 32 ] relies in practice on offline simulation calibration for each configuration; its analytic bound is too conservative for small M M and may yield no usable quantile. Our core insight is that separating an element’s set direction from its accumulation sign removes the source of this coupling. We therefore propose the random-sign IBLT. The change is lightweight: the two sides share a random-sign hash independent of the position mapping, assigning each key a random + 1 +1 or − 1 -1 . On insertion, the element’s random sign multiplies its contributions to all three fields: count, keySum, and checksum. This modification supports both decoding and estimation. Shared elements receive the same random sign in both tables and still cancel exactly after subtraction. A cell containing one unrecovered differing element has count + 1 +1 or − 1 -1 . Multiplying keySum by count cancels the random sign exactly (since ( ± 1 ) 2 = 1 (\pm 1)^{2}=1 ) and recovers the original key. Computing the key’s random sign and comparing it with count then reveals whether the key belongs to set A A or B B . Under ideal purity, the random-sign IBLT therefore peels exactly the same elements as the standard IBLT at every step. The decoding threshold, failure probability, and number and byte width of cell fields remain unchanged. For estimation, each differing element’s coding coefficient in the difference table becomes an independent uniform random sign, whether the difference is one-sided or balanced. Peeling success depends only on which cells the elements select (the mapping), while cancellation of the estimation error depends on the random signs. These are independent. For every mapping selected by failure, the random signs remain independent and uniform, so their contributions cancel in expectation. Using random signs to cancel cross terms is a classical idea from the AMS sketch and CountSketch [ 1 , 7 ] . We implement it in a peelable data structure, enabling one table to support both difference recovery and difference-size estimation and allowing rigorous statistical analysis of the post-failure estimator.

sections.heading: Main results and contributions.
sections.text: We prove that the random-sign IBLT preserves the standard IBLT’s decoding behavior under ideal purity and that the joint distribution of the difference-table statistic and the mapping is identical for all sign compositions. Section 3 presents the encoding and peeling algorithm that achieves this decoupling. We then prove that the estimator d ^ \widehat{d} is exactly unbiased on every fixed mapping, giving conditional mean d d after failure, and fully characterize the conditional distribution of the estimation error across all load scales (Sections 4 and 5 ). For large differences, we derive a Gaussian rule from the conditional Gaussian limit. For small differences, we characterize a discrete limit distribution and construct a Skellam rule whose conditional miss rate is asymptotically at most the target risk, uniformly over all difference sizes without offline simulation calibration. We also lift the known duplicate-pair mechanism to the distribution level: at low load, the failure-conditioned distribution is close in total variation to the planted distribution, which reduces the conditional analysis of rare failures to direct computation under the planted distribution and yields an efficient planted sampling method. The experiments (Section 6 ) verify that random-sign and standard encoding have identical decoding behavior. They show that the Skellam rule keeps the conditional miss rate at or below the target level within sampling error across all 189 configurations spanning several orders of magnitude in load, whereas the Gaussian rule exceeds the target by more than a factor of 8 for small differences. With this rule, the two-round protocol reliably completes synchronization at a total transmission cost close to that of an oracle using the true d d in the same protocol.

sections.heading: Structure of the paper.
sections.text: Section 2 introduces the standard IBLT model and analyzes its post-failure estimation bias. Section 3 presents the random-sign IBLT and the two-round protocol. Section 4 proves exact unbiasedness given the mapping and derives the Gaussian rule for large differences. Section 5 derives the discrete limit distribution for small differences and the Skellam rule for all scales. Section 6 reports the experimental evaluation. Sections 7 and 8 discuss related work, rule selection, and computational cost. The appendix contains complete proofs and supplementary experiments.

sections.heading: 2 Model and post-failure estimation bias
sections.text: We introduce the standard IBLT and the ideal peeling model, define the conditional miss rate required by the two-round protocol, characterize failure at low load, and explain how the standard IBLT’s post-failure bias depends on sign composition. Appendix A collects the notation used throughout the paper.

sections.heading: 2.1 The standard IBLT and the ideal peeling model
sections.text: The two sides hold sets A A and B B and seek their symmetric difference A ​ △ ​ B A\triangle B , whose size d = | A ​ △ ​ B | d=|A\triangle B| is unknown in advance. The standard IBLT consists of M M cells, each with three fields: count, keySum, and checksum. To insert a key x x , the cell hash selects k k distinct cells from [ M ] [M] and adds 1 1 , x x , and chk ⁡ ( x ) \mathrm{chk}(x) to their respective fields. Each side builds a table, and the tables are subtracted cell by cell. Shared keys contribute identical values to the same cells in both tables, so their contributions cancel in all three fields. Only the contributions of the d d differing keys remain. A key present only in A A has direction s i = + 1 s_{i}=+1 , and a key present only in B B has direction s i = − 1 s_{i}=-1 . We denote the numbers of keys in the two directions by d + d_{+} and d − d_{-} . The ordered pair ( d + , d − ) (d_{+},d_{-}) is the sign composition , and b = d + − d − = | A | − | B | b=d_{+}-d_{-}=|A|-|B| is the difference between the set sizes. We use two extreme sign compositions throughout: a one-sided difference , where all differing keys come from one side ( | b | = d |b|=d ), and a balanced difference , where both sides have the same number of differing keys ( d + = d − d_{+}=d_{-} , b = 0 b=0 ). Both correspond to common synchronization scenarios. A one-sided difference arises in one-way synchronization when only one side inserts or deletes entries. A balanced difference arises in two-way synchronization when each side modifies a small number of entries and the insertions and deletions roughly cancel. Practical loads usually lie between these extremes, depending on how much each side changes. Decoding proceeds by peeling. We repeatedly find a pure cell containing one unrecovered differing key, recover the key by multiplying keySum by count, verify it with the checksum, and remove its contribution from all k k cells it selects. Removal may make other cells pure. Peeling continues until no pure cell remains. Under ideal purity, the decoder accepts a cell as pure exactly when it contains one unrecovered differing key. Cells with count ± 1 \pm 1 that contain multiple differing keys are rejected by the checksum. Under this assumption, peeling success depends entirely on the mapping of differing keys to cells. View the M M cells as vertices and the k k cells selected by each differing key as a hyperedge. The difference table then corresponds to a random k k -uniform hypergraph: the d d differing keys independently and uniformly choose k k -subsets S i ⊆ [ M ] S_{i}\subseteq[M] , with different keys allowed to choose the same subset. We denote the unsigned mapping with key labels by 𝒢 \mathcal{G} and the overlap between two edges by H i ​ j = | S i ∩ S j | H_{ij}=|S_{i}\cap S_{j}| , the number of cells shared by differing keys i i and j j . On 𝒢 \mathcal{G} , pure cells are exactly the unsigned degree-one vertices. Peeling repeatedly deletes edges incident to these vertices. The deletion order does not affect the terminal state, which is always the hypergraph’s 2-core. A nonempty 2-core causes decoding failure, denoted by event F F , with failure probability Pr ⁡ ( F ) \Pr(F) . Thus F F depends only on the unsigned mapping 𝒢 \mathcal{G} . When the load d / M d/M is below the critical value α c \alpha_{c} (about 0.818 0.818 for k = 3 k=3 and 0.772 0.772 for k = 4 k=4 [ 26 , 12 ] ), peeling succeeds with high probability. Rare failures arise from small cores such as duplicate edge pairs, and their probability decays polynomially in M M . In the critical window of width of order M − 1 / 2 M^{-1/2} around α c \alpha_{c} , the failure probability rises from near zero to near one [ 11 ] . Above α c \alpha_{c} , the failure probability tends to one.

sections.heading: 2.2 The two-round protocol and the conditional miss rate
sections.text: Because the capacity M M must be fixed before d d is known, the two-round protocol [ 32 ] first sends a small table of fixed size M 1 M_{1} . For a small difference, peeling succeeds in the first round. After a first-round failure, the receiver obtains an upper bound U U on d d from the difference table’s count array and chooses the second-round size m ⁡ ( U ) m(U) based on U U . The second round re-encodes and decodes using a fresh, independent cell hash. Let C v C_{v} denote the count of cell v v in the difference table. Following [ 32 ] , we define the estimator d ^ \widehat{d} of d d using the count sum ∑ v C v \sum_{v}C_{v} and sum of squares ∑ v C v 2 \sum_{v}C_{v}^{2} saved before peeling begins: d ^ = 1 k ⁡ ( 1 − k / M ) ​ ( ∑ v C v 2 − 1 M ​ ( ∑ v C v ) 2 ) , \widehat{d}=\frac{1}{k(1-k/M)}\biggl(\sum_{v}C_{v}^{2}-\frac{1}{M}\Bigl(\sum_{v}C_{v}\Bigr)^{2}\biggr), (2.1) and denote its unconditional standard deviation scale by s ⁡ ( n ) s(n) : s ⁡ ( n ) = 2 ​ n ​ ( n − 1 ) M − 1 . s(n)=\sqrt{\frac{2n(n-1)}{M-1}}. (2.2) For the standard IBLT, d ^ \widehat{d} is exactly unbiased for d d and has variance s ​ ( d ) 2 s(d)^{2} for every sign composition. This expectation is unconditional: it averages over all runs, regardless of failure F F . If we evaluated the upper bound U U over all runs, adding a few standard deviations to d ^ \widehat{d} would control the underestimate probability. In the two-round protocol, a successful first round ends the protocol immediately, without computing U U . Only after decoding failure (event F F ) does the receiver compute U U to size the second-round table. If U < d U<d , the second-round capacity falls below the prescribed margin, risking another failure. We call the event U < d U<d a miss and its probability conditioned on first-round failure, Pr ⁡ ( U < d ∣ F ) \Pr(U<d\mid F) , the conditional miss rate . The sizing rule must therefore satisfy Pr ⁡ ( U < d ∣ F ) ≤ u , \Pr(U<d\mid F)\leq u, (2.3) where u u is the target risk. In deployment, we can choose 0.01 0.01 or 0.05 0.05 , corresponding to a 1 % or 5 % underestimate risk. The two-round protocol incurs a miss only when the first round fails and the upper bound underestimates d d . This event has joint miss rate Pr ⁡ ( F , U < d ) = Pr ⁡ ( F ) ​ Pr ⁡ ( U < d ∣ F ) \Pr(F,\,U<d)=\Pr(F)\Pr(U<d\mid F) . Controlling the conditional miss rate at u u bounds the joint miss rate by u ​ Pr ⁡ ( F ) u\Pr(F) , both in overload, where failure is almost certain, and at low load, where it is rare. For failure samples without a miss ( U ≥ d U\geq d ), the second-round table has sufficient capacity margin to decode with high probability. Section 5.5 gives the complete decomposition of the total two-round failure rate.

sections.heading: 2.3 Failure at low load and the planted distribution
sections.text: Eq. ( 2.3 ) must hold at all loads. Low load requires separate treatment. When d d is much smaller than M M , the failure probability decays polynomially in M M . Failure is then rare, making the distribution conditioned on F F difficult to analyze directly and requiring many simulated mappings for each failure sample. The structure of failure in this region is simple. Two edges with the same mapping form a duplicate edge pair. A single edge cannot form a 2-core, and two edges form a 2-core exactly when they are a duplicate edge pair. When d = o ⁡ ( M ) d=o(M) , 2-cores with three or more edges are negligible relative to duplicate edge pairs. Failure is therefore approximately equivalent to the existence of a duplicate edge pair. Conditioning on F F is close to planting a duplicate edge pair in a random mapping. We thus define the planted distribution : choose a pair of keys uniformly, assign both the same uniformly random k k -subset, and let all remaining keys choose their mappings independently and uniformly. Proposition 2.1 (Failure is determined by duplicate edge pairs when d = o ⁡ ( M ) d=o(M) ) . Fix k ≥ 3 k\geq 3 and let 2 ≤ d = o ⁡ ( M ) 2\leq d=o(M) . The failure probability is asymptotically equal to the expected number of duplicate edge pairs: Pr ⁡ ( F ) ∼ ( d 2 ) / ( M k ) \Pr(F)\sim\binom{d}{2}/\binom{M}{k} . The total variation distance between the distribution of 𝒢 \mathcal{G} conditioned on F F and the planted distribution tends to zero. Goodrich and Mitzenmacher [ 17 ] identify duplicate edge pairs as the main source of IBLT failure. The finite-length analysis of Yugawa and Wadayama [ 34 ] likewise shows that stopping sets of size 2 dominate. Proposition 2.1 extends this observation to a total variation approximation of the entire mapping for all d = o ⁡ ( M ) d=o(M) . Lemma D.2 in Appendix D gives the quantitative error bound and proof. Proposition 2.1 supports both theory and experiments. It replaces conditioning on failure with the planted distribution, under which direct calculations are straightforward. The limit theorems in Sections 4 and 5 use this approximation to handle conditioning on failure when d = o ⁡ ( M ) d=o(M) . The risk decomposition in Section 5.5 also uses it to estimate the first-round failure probability. For experiments, it enables direct sampling from the planted distribution, where every sample yields a failure. Section 6.1 uses this planted sampling to evaluate low-load configurations beyond the reach of direct sampling and checks its finite-size accuracy where both methods are feasible.

sections.heading: 2.4 Post-failure bias of the standard IBLT
sections.text: Controlling Eq. ( 2.3 ) is difficult because the failure event F F selects the mapping 𝒢 \mathcal{G} . This selection changes the distribution of the overlaps H i ​ j H_{ij} . At low load, failure samples mainly contain duplicate edge pairs (Proposition 2.1 ), whose overlap is k k , increasing the conditional mean of H i ​ j H_{ij} . In the critical window and at higher load, failure corresponds to mappings with large cores. Such a core is a local structure, and the direction of the change in the conditional mean of H i ​ j H_{ij} depends on k k , as measured by c F c_{F} below. Statistics that depend on H i ​ j H_{ij} therefore require separate analysis after conditioning on F F . In the standard IBLT, the difference-table count is C v = ∑ i : v ∈ S i s i C_{v}=\sum_{i:v\in S_{i}}s_{i} , and each differing key’s coding coefficient is its fixed set direction s i ∈ { + 1 , − 1 } s_{i}\in\{+1,-1\} . In the sum of C v 2 C_{v}^{2} , the diagonal terms contribute exactly k ​ d kd . The estimation error comes entirely from the cross terms s i ​ s j ​ H i ​ j s_{i}s_{j}H_{ij} between keys sharing cells. Excess overlap raises d ^ \widehat{d} for same-sign pairs and lowers d ^ \widehat{d} for opposite-sign pairs. The conditional relative bias of d ^ \widehat{d} thus factors exactly into two terms. This suggests encoding differing keys with independent, uniform random signs so that every cross term has zero mean for each mapping, while preserving peeling’s ability to recover each key’s original set direction. sections.heading: 3 The random-sign IBLT
sections.text: We introduce the random-sign IBLT. The design multiplies each key by a random sign shared by both sides during insertion and deletion. The cell fields, field widths, and peeling process remain unchanged. We first give the encoding and decoding rules and prove ideal decoding equivalence with the standard IBLT and independence of the coding coefficients from the mapping. We then explain how the two-round protocol uses the lower bound | b | |b| to determine the second-round capacity.

sections.heading: 3.1 Encoding rules, decoding equivalence, and sign independence
sections.text: The two sides agree in advance on a sign hash ε : 𝒰 → { − 1 , + 1 } \varepsilon:\mathcal{U}\to\{-1,+1\} independent of the cell hash. Each sign is generated directly from the key and a shared seed, requiring no per-key storage. Algorithm 3.1 gives the complete encoding and decoding procedure. The lines marked ⋆ \star show all changes from the standard IBLT: applying the sign during insertion and deletion and recovering the direction on output. The number of cell fields, field widths, and peeling control flow remain unchanged. We describe encoding and decoding in turn. Algorithm 3.1 Encoding and decoding of the random-sign IBLT. To insert a key x x , we add ε ⁡ ( x ) \varepsilon(x) , ε ⁡ ( x ) ​ x \varepsilon(x)\,x , and ε ⁡ ( x ) ​ chk ​ ( x ) \varepsilon(x)\,\mathrm{chk}(x) to the three fields of each of its k k cells. Deletion subtracts the same quantities. We accumulate keySum and checksum modulo 2 64 2^{64} . In the set model, these two fields also support the bitwise XOR implementation commonly used in the standard IBLT (Appendix C.1 ). Our analysis and experiments use the additive form. Subtracting the two tables cell by cell cancels the identical contributions of each shared key in all three fields. A differing key i i has coding coefficient s i ​ ε i s_{i}\varepsilon_{i} in the difference table, where ε i = ε ⁡ ( x i ) \varepsilon_{i}=\varepsilon(x_{i}) . Thus, cell v v in the difference table has fields C v = ∑ i : v ∈ S i s i ε i , keySum v = ∑ i : v ∈ S i s i ε i x i , checksum v = ∑ i : v ∈ S i s i ε i chk ( x i ) . C_{v}=\sum_{i:v\in S_{i}}s_{i}\varepsilon_{i},\qquad\mathrm{keySum}_{v}=\sum_{i:v\in S_{i}}s_{i}\varepsilon_{i}\,x_{i},\qquad\mathrm{checksum}_{v}=\sum_{i:v\in S_{i}}s_{i}\varepsilon_{i}\,\mathrm{chk}(x_{i}). (3.1) We treat ε i \varepsilon_{i} as iid uniform signs independent of the mapping 𝒢 \mathcal{G} . Decoding follows lines 8–17 and uses the standard IBLT peeling process. A pure cell v v containing a single unrecovered differing key x i x_{i} has count C v = s i ​ ε i ∈ { − 1 , + 1 } C_{v}=s_{i}\varepsilon_{i}\in\{-1,+1\} . Multiplying keySum v \mathrm{keySum}_{v} by C v C_{v} cancels the sign s i ​ ε i s_{i}\varepsilon_{i} and yields the candidate key x i x_{i} (line 12). Once the candidate passes the checksum and cell-membership checks (line 13), we multiply C v C_{v} by ε ⁡ ( x i ) \varepsilon(x_{i}) . sections.heading: 3.2 The two-round protocol flow and the lower bound | b | |b|
sections.text: In the two-round protocol, the receiver subtracts the tables cell by cell and runs peeling on the difference table. For the standard IBLT, the count sum 1 k ​ ∑ v C v = b = d + − d − \frac{1}{k}\sum_{v}C_{v}=b=d_{+}-d_{-} directly gives the deterministic lower bound d ≥ | b | d\geq|b| . The sender therefore attaches the set size | A | |A| (8 bytes) to the first-round table, allowing the receiver to compute b = | A | − | B | b=|A|-|B| directly. If first-round peeling succeeds, the protocol ends immediately. After a first-round failure, the receiver computes an upper bound U U from the raw counts ( C v ) (C_{v}) of the difference table. The computation uses only the two scalars ∑ v C v 2 \sum_{v}C_{v}^{2} and ∑ v C v \sum_{v}C_{v} , which the receiver accumulates while subtracting cells one by one, and peeling can modify the difference table in place. It incorporates the known lower bound | b | |b| by taking U b = max ⁡ ( U , | b | ) U_{b}=\max(U,|b|) (for a one-sided difference, | b | = d |b|=d ). The second-round table has size m ⁡ ( U b ) = ⌈ U b / ( 0.8 ​ α c ) ⌉ m(U_{b})=\lceil U_{b}/(0.8\alpha_{c})\rceil . We re-encode and decode using a fresh cell hash independent of the first round. Whenever U b ≥ d U_{b}\geq d , the second-round load is at most 0.8 ​ α c 0.8\alpha_{c} , leaving a margin below the peeling threshold. The second round therefore succeeds with high probability. The analysis applies to any constant target load below α c \alpha_{c} ; we use 0.8. Sections 4 and 5 analyze the post-failure distribution of the sum of squared counts and give the rule for computing U U .

sections.heading: 4 Unbiased estimation after failure and the Gaussian upper bound
sections.text: We use the independence of signs and mapping established in Section 3 to analyze d ^ \widehat{d} after decoding failure and construct an upper bound for d d . Cancellation between random signs of different keys makes d ^ \widehat{d} exactly unbiased for every fixed mapping (Proposition 4.1 ). It therefore remains unbiased even after arbitrarily rare failures. Controlling the conditional miss rate at the target risk u u also requires the distribution of post-failure fluctuations of d ^ \widehat{d} around d d . When d ≫ M d\gg\sqrt{M} , the standardized estimation error converges to the standard Gaussian distribution (Theorem 4.2 ), yielding the Gaussian rule (Definition 4.3 ).

sections.heading: 4.1 Conditional unbiasedness and conditional variance given the mapping
sections.text: We expand the sum of squares and the total sum in Eq. ( 2.1 ) by key. Each differing key occupies k k cells and satisfies ε i 2 = 1 \varepsilon_{i}^{2}=1 , so the diagonal contributions of the two terms sum to exactly d d . The estimation error consists of the cross terms between different keys: d ^ − d = 2 k ⁡ ( 1 − k / M ) ​ ∑ i < j ε i ​ ε j ​ ( H i ​ j − k 2 M ) . \widehat{d}-d=\frac{2}{k(1-k/M)}\sum_{i<j}\varepsilon_{i}\varepsilon_{j}\Bigl(H_{ij}-\frac{k^{2}}{M}\Bigr). (4.1) The right-hand side is a quadratic form in the random signs. Each coefficient H i ​ j − k 2 / M H_{ij}-k^{2}/M measures the overlap relative to its unconditional mean and depends entirely on the mapping 𝒢 \mathcal{G} . For the standard IBLT, the same expansion replaces the sign products with fixed values s i ​ s j s_{i}s_{j} . Selection of overlaps by failure then translates directly into bias (Proposition 2.2 ). With random signs, each ε i ​ ε j \varepsilon_{i}\varepsilon_{j} takes ± 1 \pm 1 with equal probability even on a fixed mapping where failure occurs (Proposition 3.2 ). The cross terms therefore have mean zero on every mapping. Intuitively, failure selects the mapping and hence the cross-term coefficients, while each sign product remains equally likely to be positive or negative. The error remains centered at zero, while its conditional variance can change. Proposition 4.1 expresses this intuition through the conditional mean and variance given the mapping. Proposition 4.1 (Conditional unbiasedness and conditional moments given the mapping) . For every fixed mapping 𝒢 \mathcal{G} , 𝔼 ⁡ [ d ^ ∣ 𝒢 ] = d , Var ⁡ ( d ^ ∣ 𝒢 ) = 4 k 2 ​ ( 1 − k / M ) 2 ​ ∑ i < j ( H i ​ j − k 2 M ) 2 ≤ 2 ​ d ​ ( d − 1 ) . \mathbb{E}[\widehat{d}\mid\mathcal{G}]=d,\qquad\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{d}\mid\mathcal{G})=\frac{4}{k^{2}(1-k/M)^{2}}\sum_{i<j}\Bigl(H_{ij}-\frac{k^{2}}{M}\Bigr)^{2}\leq 2d(d-1). (4.2) Thus, for any mapping event 𝒮 \mathcal{S} of positive probability, 𝔼 ⁡ [ d ^ ∣ 𝒮 ] = d \mathbb{E}[\widehat{d}\mid\mathcal{S}]=d . In particular, 𝔼 ⁡ [ d ^ ∣ F ] = d \mathbb{E}[\widehat{d}\mid F]=d holds for every finite M M and every sign composition, even for arbitrarily rare failures. Averaging over the random mapping 𝒢 \mathcal{G} gives 𝔼 ​ d ^ = d \mathbb{E}\widehat{d}=d and Var ⁡ d ^ = s ​ ( d ) 2 \operatorname{Var}\widehat{d}=s(d)^{2} . Proof sketch. Given 𝒢 \mathcal{G} , ( ε i ) (\varepsilon_{i}) are iid uniform signs. Taking expectations term by term in Eq. ( 4.1 ) and using 𝔼 ⁡ [ ε i ​ ε j ∣ 𝒢 ] = 0 \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{i}\varepsilon_{j}\mid\mathcal{G}]=0 proves conditional unbiasedness. The sign products for distinct unordered pairs ( i , j ) (i,j) are pairwise uncorrelated, yielding the conditional variance in Eq. ( 4.2 ). The full proof is in Appendix C.3 . ∎ For a fixed mapping, d ^ \widehat{d} is a Rademacher quadratic form with the Gram matrix of the centered incidence vectors. Its conditional mean equals the trace, and its conditional variance comes only from the off-diagonal terms. These are the same identities used by the Hutchinson trace estimator [ 18 ] . sections.heading: 4.2 The Gaussian limit after failure when d ≫ M d\gg\sqrt{M}
sections.text: Proposition 4.1 establishes the center of the estimator after failure. Constructing an upper bound also requires the shape of the error distribution around this center. Failure affects d ^ \widehat{d} only through the mapping. By Eq. ( 4.2 ), the sum of squared overlaps ∑ i < j ( H i ​ j − k 2 / M ) 2 \sum_{i<j}(H_{ij}-k^{2}/M)^{2} determines the conditional error scale. Failure selects mappings with different values of this sum and may therefore change the error distribution. We first fix a mapping. By Eq. ( 4.1 ), the error is a weighted sum of sign products ε i ​ ε j \varepsilon_{i}\varepsilon_{j} . The main contributions come from key pairs sharing a cell: the intersecting edge pairs with H i ​ j ≥ 1 H_{ij}\geq 1 in 𝒢 \mathcal{G} . Their expected number is about k 2 ​ d 2 / ( 2 ​ M ) k^{2}d^{2}/(2M) . Sign products for distinct key pairs are pairwise uncorrelated, and no small set of terms dominates the sum. The number of intersecting edge pairs grows with d 2 / M d^{2}/M and tends to infinity when d ≫ M d\gg\sqrt{M} . Under a subcritical load, a typical failure is caused by a duplicate edge pair. This raises a single H i ​ j H_{ij} to k k and leaves the overall structure of intersecting edge pairs almost unchanged. Theorem 4.2 (Gaussian limit after failure) . Fix k ≥ 3 k\geq 3 and let d / M → ∞ d/\sqrt{M}\to\infty , allowing any limiting behavior of d / M d/M . Then sup x | Pr ⁡ ( X ≤ x ∣ F ) − Φ ⁡ ( x ) | ⟶ 0 . \sup_{x}\bigl|\Pr(X\leq x\mid F)-\Phi(x)\bigr|\longrightarrow 0. (4.5) This includes the critical window, rare failures under a fixed subcritical load, and arbitrary overload. Proof sketch. The proof has two steps. First, we fix the mapping and take randomness only over the signs. Suppose the number of intersecting edge pairs is of the same order as M M , the ratio of the sum of squared overlaps Ω 2 = ∑ i < j H i ​ j 2 \Omega_{2}=\sum_{i<j}H_{ij}^{2} to its exact mean tends to one, and each key participates in overlaps of size at most O ⁡ ( log ⁡ M ) O(\log M) . Second, we show that, conditional on F F , the mapping satisfies these conditions with probability tending to 1 1 . We consider three cases according to the limit of d / M d/M . When d / M d/M has a positive finite limit, Pr ⁡ ( F ) ≥ ( M k ) − 1 \Pr(F)\geq\binom{M}{k}^{-1} . sections.heading: 4.3 The Gaussian rule and its conditional miss rate
sections.text: By Theorem 4.2 , d ^ \widehat{d} is approximately Gaussian after failure, with mean d d and standard deviation s ⁡ ( d ) s(d) . If d d were known, we could set the margin using the fact that d ^ \widehat{d} falls below d + s ⁡ ( d ) ​ Φ − 1 ​ ( u ) d+s(d)\Phi^{-1}(u) with probability about u u . However, the scale s ⁡ ( d ) s(d) (Eq. ( 2.2 )) depends on the unknown d d . Direct substitution of s ⁡ ( d ^ ) s(\widehat{d}) would make the margin fluctuate with the observation. A low d ^ \widehat{d} gives a small s ⁡ ( d ^ ) s(\widehat{d}) , reducing the margin precisely for samples that need a larger one. The risk analysis would then need to account for this additional error. Test inversion is a classical method for constructing confidence sets [ 27 ] . We reverse the reasoning and test candidate values individually. For each candidate n n , we assume the true value is n n . The scale s ⁡ ( n ) s(n) is then known, and d ^ \widehat{d} falls below n + s ⁡ ( n ) ​ Φ − 1 ​ ( u ) n+s(n)\Phi^{-1}(u) with probability about u u . An observation below this lower bound indicates that n n is too large, so we exclude n n . The largest remaining candidate gives the upper bound U U . The risk is controlled by a single event: U < d U<d implies that the true value d d is excluded. Under the true value d d , this exclusion has probability about u u . Given an observation d ^ \widehat{d} and a target risk u ∈ ( 0 , 1 / 2 ) u\in(0,1/2) , we test each candidate integer n ≥ 2 n\geq 2 as the true value, for which the scale s ⁡ ( n ) s(n) is known. Let χ M − 1 , u 2 \chi^{2}_{M-1,u} denote the lower u u quantile of the chi-square distribution with M − 1 M-1 degrees of freedom. Set the acceptance lower bound to t ⁡ ( n ) = n + s ⁡ ( n ) ​ χ M − 1 , u 2 − ( M − 1 ) 2 ​ ( M − 1 ) . t(n)=n+s(n)\,\frac{\chi^{2}_{M-1,u}-(M-1)}{\sqrt{2(M-1)}}. (4.6) We accept candidate n n if d ^ ≥ t ⁡ ( n ) \widehat{d}\geq t(n) and reject it otherwise. We set U U to the largest accepted candidate, returning + ∞ +\infty if none is accepted. For fixed M , k M,k as d → ∞ d\to\infty , d ^ / d \widehat{d}/d converges in distribution to χ 2 ​ ( M − 1 ) / ( M − 1 ) \chi^{2}(M-1)/(M-1) [ 32 ] , which has mean 1. sections.heading: 5 The Skellam rule for all loads
sections.text: The Gaussian rule’s conditional miss rate guarantee requires d ≫ M d\gg\sqrt{M} . If we size the IBLT table for the expected load, d d can be far below M \sqrt{M} . Failure is then rare, but the two-round protocol must still use the post-failure observation to size the second-round table. In this range, the conditional miss rate of the Gaussian rule can be several times the target u u (Table H.7 in the appendix). The reason lies in the shape of the post-failure error at low load. Failure then has essentially one source: two differing keys select exactly the same k k cells. The duplicate edge pair itself forms a 2-core. Even after the remaining keys have been peeled, these two keys remain. Under random signs, the two keys are equally likely to have the same or opposite signs. If we place each key in the table alone, it leaves a count of ± 1 \pm 1 in each of its k k cells. Together, their squared counts sum to 2 ​ k 2k . Dividing by k k gives their exact contribution of 2 2 . With opposite signs, the counts in all k k shared cells cancel to 0 0 . The entire sum of squares of 2 ​ k 2k disappears, leaving the estimate 2 2 below the true value. With equal signs, each shared cell has count ± 2 \pm 2 and squared count 4 4 . The sum of squares becomes 4 ​ k 4k , leaving the estimate 2 2 above the true value. This jump is equally likely to be upward or downward, and its size is independent of M M . The remaining keys also occasionally share a cell, almost always exactly one. Each such overlap shifts the estimate by 2 / k 2/k , again with either direction equally likely. The number of such key pairs is approximately Poisson [ 2 ] and remains finite when c c is bounded. The post-failure error thus consists of one large jump of size 2 2 and several small jumps of size 2 / k 2/k . The Gaussian approximation cannot capture these two types of jumps. When d d is small relative to M \sqrt{M} , the standard deviation s ⁡ ( d ) s(d) of the Gaussian rule tends to zero. The downward jump of size 2 2 remains unchanged and lies arbitrarily many standard deviations into the Gaussian tail. The probability of rejecting the true value therefore tends to one half. When c c is of order one, only finitely many small jumps occur. The error still has a lattice distribution, with a visible departure from the Gaussian in the lower tail corresponding to the target risk (Appendix H.6 ). We construct a null distribution that retains both types of jumps and approaches the Gaussian used by the Gaussian rule as c c grows (Figure 5.1 ). The resulting Skellam rule controls the conditional miss rate for all d ≥ 2 d\geq 2 . Appendices F and G give the full proof and numerical implementation.

sections.heading: 5.1 The lattice-preserving test statistic d ~ \widetilde{d}
sections.text: To keep these jumps exactly on lattice points, we need a discrete test statistic. The correction term ( ∑ v C v ) 2 / M (\sum_{v}C_{v})^{2}/M in d ^ \widehat{d} shifts its values off the lattice. We therefore use the normalized sum of squares without subtracting the mean term, d ~ = 1 k ​ ∑ v = 1 M C v 2 . \widetilde{d}=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{v=1}^{M}C_{v}^{2}. (5.1) Expanding the sum of squares gives d d from the diagonal terms, leaving only overlap contributions to the error: d ~ − d = 2 k ​ ∑ i < j H i ​ j ​ ε i ​ ε j . \widetilde{d}-d=\frac{2}{k}\sum_{i<j}H_{ij}\,\varepsilon_{i}\varepsilon_{j}. (5.2) Every term on the right is an integer multiple of 2 / k 2/k , so d ~ − d \widetilde{d}-d takes only integer multiples of 2 / k 2/k . The expansion shows both types of jumps directly. A duplicate edge pair has H i ​ j = k H_{ij}=k and contributes exactly 2 ​ ε i ​ ε j 2\varepsilon_{i}\varepsilon_{j} , or ± 2 \pm 2 with equal probability. An edge pair sharing a single cell has H i ​ j = 1 H_{ij}=1 and contributes ± 2 / k \pm 2/k . Without the correction term, d ~ \widetilde{d} remains exactly unbiased for every mapping. Proposition 5.1 (Conditional unbiasedness of d ~ \widetilde{d} ) . For every fixed mapping 𝒢 \mathcal{G} , 𝔼 ⁡ [ d ~ ∣ 𝒢 ] = d \mathbb{E}[\widetilde{d}\mid\mathcal{G}]=d . Thus, for any mapping event 𝒮 \mathcal{S} with positive probability, 𝔼 ⁡ [ d ~ ∣ 𝒮 ] = d \mathbb{E}[\widetilde{d}\mid\mathcal{S}]=d . In particular, 𝔼 ⁡ [ d ~ ∣ F ] = d \mathbb{E}[\widetilde{d}\mid F]=d holds for all finite M M and all sign compositions, however rare the failure. Proof. Given 𝒢 \mathcal{G} , H i ​ j H_{ij} is constant. By Proposition 3.2 , the signs remain iid and uniform, so 𝔼 ⁡ [ ε i ​ ε j ∣ 𝒢 ] = 0 \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{i}\varepsilon_{j}\mid\mathcal{G}]=0 for i ≠ j i\neq j . Taking expectations term by term in Eq. ( 5.2 ) gives the result. ∎ This property also follows from the random signs. In the standard IBLT, the cross terms have fixed sign products s i ​ s j s_{i}s_{j} . The same expansion gives the unconditional mean of the sum of squares as d + k M ​ ( b 2 − d ) d+\frac{k}{M}(b^{2}-d) , which depends on the unknown b b . The correction term in d ^ \widehat{d} removes this dependence. With random signs, the cross terms have mean zero for every mapping. sections.heading: 5.4 The Skellam rule controls the conditional miss rate at all loads
sections.text: The Skellam rule uses the test inversion of the Gaussian rule (Section 4.3 ), replacing the Gaussian lower tail with the lattice lower tail of G n G_{n} . If the observation falls in the lower u u tail of G n G_{n} , candidate n n is too large to be the true value, so we reject candidate n n . We take U U to be the largest accepted candidate. Definition 5.5 (Skellam rule) . Let d ~ \widetilde{d} be the observation and u ∈ ( 0 , 1 / 2 ) u\in(0,1/2) the target risk. For each candidate integer n ≥ 2 n\geq 2 , we accept n n if G n ​ ( d ~ ) > u G_{n}(\widetilde{d})>u and reject it otherwise. We define the upper bound as the supremum of all accepted candidates, U = sup { n ≥ 2 : G n ​ ( d ~ ) > u } , U=\sup\bigl\{n\geq 2:\ G_{n}(\widetilde{d})>u\bigr\}, (5.8) with U = + ∞ U=+\infty when the accepted candidates are unbounded. The null distribution for candidate 2 2 takes only the values 0 0 and 4 4 . Since d ~ ≥ 0 \widetilde{d}\geq 0 , we always accept candidate 2 2 , so U ≥ 2 U\geq 2 . For practical table sizes, U U is also finite (for u = 0.01 u=0.01 , M > 18 M>18 suffices). We can compute it exactly by a finite search, at a cost roughly proportional to λ d \lambda_{d} per computation (Appendix G ). The behavior of the Skellam rule at small and large loads explains why it applies throughout. Consider first small c c . The Skellam term is then almost zero, the error after failure comes almost entirely from the duplicate edge pair, and the observation d ~ \widetilde{d} equals d − 2 d-2 or d + 2 d+2 with probability one half each. The scale s ⁡ ( n ) s(n) of the Gaussian rule tends to zero in this region, so its upper bound U U stays close to the observation. When the duplicate edge pair has opposite signs, the observation is d − 2 d-2 , U U falls below d d , and the conditional miss rate tends to one half. The null distribution G n G_{n} of the Skellam rule retains this structure and assigns half its mass to n − 2 n-2 and half to n + 2 n+2 . We accept candidate n n exactly when the smaller value n − 2 n-2 does not exceed the observation, giving U ≈ d ~ + 2 U\approx\widetilde{d}+2 . The rule thus adds back a potentially lost large jump. With opposite signs, U U equals d d exactly; with equal signs, U U is about d + 4 d+4 . Neither case produces a miss. Consider next large c c . The Skellam term then dominates and G n G_{n} approaches the Gaussian used by the Gaussian rule, so the two rules give the same upper bound, and the Gaussian rule already controls the conditional miss rate in this region (Corollary 4.4 ). Theorem 5.6 gives the main result of this section. As the table size tends to infinity, the probability that the Skellam rule underestimates d d after failure is asymptotically at most the target risk u u , uniformly over all d ≥ 2 d\geq 2 . This guarantee holds for any sign composition. The rule uses only ∑ v C v 2 \sum_{v}C_{v}^{2} from the same table and the known parameters ( M , k , u ) (M,k,u) . The Gaussian rule provides this guarantee only when d ≫ M d\gg\sqrt{M} (Corollary 4.4 ). In Section 5.5 , we apply this guarantee to the risk decomposition of the two-round protocol. Theorem 5.6 (Uniform asymptotic upper bound on the conditional miss rate) . Fix k ≥ 3 k\geq 3 and u ∈ ( 0 , 1 / 2 ) u\in(0,1/2) . For any sign composition, the Skellam rule satisfies lim sup M → ∞ sup d ≥ 2 Pr ⁡ ( U < d ∣ F ) ≤ u . \limsup_{M\to\infty}\ \sup_{d\geq 2}\ \Pr(U<d\mid F)\leq u. (5.9) Proof sketch. If the observation has distribution G n G_{n} exactly, we reject n n when it falls in a lower tail with total probability at most u u . By the definition of the CDF, the rejection probability is at most u u , including for discrete distributions. The rejection region is a lower set, so the rejection probabilities under the actual distribution and G n G_{n} differ by at most their Kolmogorov distance. A miss implies rejection of the true value: { U < d } ⊆ { G d ( d ~ ) ≤ u } \{U<d\}\subseteq\{G_{d}(\widetilde{d})\leq u\} . Taking n = d n=d and applying Theorem 5.4 gives Eq. ( 5.9 ). By Proposition 3.2 , the joint distribution of the coding coefficients is independent of the sign composition. The result therefore holds for any sign composition. Appendix F.4 gives the full proof. ∎ Theorem 5.6 is asymptotic in the table size. Two effects arise on finite tables. First, G n G_{n} is a lattice distribution, so the rejection region contains only whole probability masses. The actual conditional miss rate can therefore be strictly below u u . Second, the null distribution omits overlaps between the duplicate edge pair and the remaining keys. Each of the other d − 2 d-2 keys has a cell among the k k cells of the pair with probability about k 2 / M k^{2}/M , so these overlaps occur at a total rate of about ( d − 2 ) ​ k 2 / M (d-2)k^{2}/M . They can push the conditional miss rate slightly above u u on small tables. Section 6.4 evaluates finite-table behavior experimentally (Figures 6.4 and 6.5 ). At M = 64 M=64 , the largest miss/u is 1.08, an excess beyond sampling error. All configurations with M ≥ 256 M\geq 256 meet the target within sampling error. At fixed c c , this occurrence rate is about c ​ k 2 / M ck^{2}/\sqrt{M} . The omitted overlaps become rarer as M M grows, and extra capacity decreases as well. When the first-round table must be small, the second-round sizing margin 1 / ( 0.8 ​ α c ) 1/(0.8\alpha_{c}) absorbs slight underestimation (Section 5.5 ). If more margin is needed, we can reduce the target load from 0.8, using a larger second-round table to lower the two-round failure rate.

sections.heading: 5.5 From the conditional miss rate to the failure probability of the two-round protocol
sections.text: We now connect the post-failure conditional miss rate to the overall success rate of two-round reconciliation. The protocol follows Section 3.2 . We denote first-round failure by F 1 F_{1} and second-round failure by F 2 F_{2} . Let E E denote a checksum error: a non-pure cell passes the check, a key that passes the check lies outside the set difference, or all fields are zero at termination despite a nonempty core. Theorem 5.7 (Two-round risk decomposition) . Under the ideal hash model, let Pr m ⁡ ( F ) \Pr_{m}(F) denote the probability of peeling failure for d d differing keys in a fresh table with m m cells. Then Pr ⁡ ( ( F 1 ∩ F 2 ) ∪ E ) ≤ Pr ⁡ ( F 1 , U b < d ) + Pr ⁡ ( F 1 ) ​ max m ≥ m ⁡ ( d ) ​ Pr m ⁡ ( F ) + Pr ⁡ ( F 1 , U b = + ∞ ) + Pr ⁡ ( E ) . \Pr\big((F_{1}\cap F_{2})\cup E\big)\leq\Pr(F_{1},\ U_{b}<d)+\Pr(F_{1})\max_{m\geq m(d)}\Pr\nolimits_{m}(F)+\Pr(F_{1},\ U_{b}=+\infty)+\Pr(E). (5.10) Proof. By the union bound, it suffices to bound F 1 ∩ F 2 F_{1}\cap F_{2} and E E separately. The upper bound U b U_{b} is a function of the first-round counts and the set sizes. The second-round mapping is independent of it. Under ideal purity, F 2 F_{2} depends only on the second-round mapping and d d . On { U b < d } \{U_{b}<d\} and { U b = + ∞ } \{U_{b}=+\infty\} , we bound the conditional second-round failure probability by one. On { d ≤ U b < + ∞ } \{d\leq U_{b}<+\infty\} , we have m ⁡ ( U b ) ≥ m ⁡ ( d ) m(U_{b})\geq m(d) and the conditional second-round failure probability is Pr m ⁡ ( U b ) ⁡ ( F ) ≤ max m ≥ m ⁡ ( d ) ⁡ Pr m ⁡ ( F ) \Pr_{m(U_{b})}(F)\leq\max_{m\geq m(d)}\Pr_{m}(F) . Adding the parts gives Eq. ( 5.10 ). ∎ The first two of the four terms are the core risks. The first is a sizing error, the joint miss rate Pr ⁡ ( F 1 ) ​ Pr ⁡ ( U b < d ∣ F 1 ) \Pr(F_{1})\Pr(U_{b}<d\mid F_{1}) : for the Skellam rule it is asymptotically at most u ​ Pr ⁡ ( F 1 ) u\Pr(F_{1}) uniformly (Theorem 5.6 ), and it is zero for a one-sided difference; the Gaussian rule has a larger conditional miss rate when c c is bounded, but failure itself is then rare. The second is a failure of second-round peeling with sufficient capacity; the second-round load is at most 0.8 ​ α c 0.8\alpha_{c} , and this term decays polynomially in d d (Lemma D.3 ). The last two terms are marginal. The third is the absence of a finite upper bound: the Skellam rule never produces it when M 1 > 4 ​ log ⁡ ( 1 / u ) M_{1}>4\log(1/u) , and the Gaussian rule essentially only for d = 2 d=2 or 3 3 . As an example, take k = 3 k=3 , M 1 = 1024 M_{1}=1024 , d = 838 d=838 ( d / M 1 ≈ 0.82 d/M_{1}\approx 0.82 , corresponding to first-round load d / ( α c ​ M 1 ) = 1 d/(\alpha_{c}M_{1})=1 in Section 6 ), u = 0.01 u=0.01 , and a balanced difference. In the protocol experiments ( Exp-PROTO ) of Section 6.5 , 19,187 of 26,667 trials fail in the first round, giving Pr ⁡ ( F 1 ) ≈ 0.72 \Pr(F_{1})\approx 0.72 . sections.heading: 6 Experimental evaluation
sections.text: The experiments address three questions. First, does random-sign encoding remove the dependence of the post-failure estimate on sign composition while preserving decoding (Section 6.2 )? Second, what is the shape of the post-failure statistic’s lower tail (Section 6.3 ), and how does this shape determine the conditional miss rate and extra capacity of the two rules at finite size (Section 6.4 )? Third, when the upper bound is used in a two-round protocol on a complete IBLT, what are the reliability and communication cost (Section 6.5 ), what is the computational cost, and how do these results guide rule choice (Section 6.6 )? The experiments fall into two categories. The first uses only a peeling sampler, without constructing a complete IBLT, to study the distribution of the post-failure statistic. Its main component is the statistical experiments ( Exp-STAT ), configured as in Section 6.1 ; the planted-sampling control ( Exp-PLANT ), conditional-unbiasedness test ( Exp-UNB ), and worst-configuration test ( Exp-WORST ) verify planted sampling, conditional unbiasedness, and the configurations with the highest risk, respectively. The second category uses complete IBLTs. The protocol experiments ( Exp-PROTO ) run the two-round protocol, configured as in Section 6.5 ; the decoding-equivalence test ( Exp-DEC ) and computational-cost measurement ( Exp-COST ) verify decoding results and measure time and memory, respectively. Appendix H.1 summarizes each experiment’s purpose and scale. The main conclusions are measured on failure samples, and failure probabilities vary by orders of magnitude across configurations. Before launch, a single feasibility pilot estimates each configuration’s failure probability. We use these estimates to set the trial counts needed to collect enough failures, targeting about 20,000 for the statistical and protocol experiments, and use planted sampling when direct sampling is too costly (Section 6.1 ). We then fix configurations, seeds, stopping rules, and sample sizes, with no adjustments during the formal runs. A few figures and tables use an additional single configuration to illustrate the distribution’s shape, with parameters given in the caption.

sections.heading: 6.1 Configurations and sampling for the statistical experiments
sections.text: The statistical experiments use a sampler that independently generates d d uniform random hyperedges and runs peeling, without constructing a complete IBLT. On each mapping, we compute X = ( d ^ − d ) / s ⁡ ( d ) X=(\widehat{d}-d)/s(d) for the standard encoding under one-sided and balanced differences, together with the exact integers ∑ v C v \sum_{v}C_{v} and ∑ v C v 2 \sum_{v}C_{v}^{2} for the random-sign encoding. We then compute both rules’ upper bounds from the same observation. Each configuration is specified by ( k , M , d ) (k,M,d) . We describe its position along two axes: c = d / M c=d/\sqrt{M} (Eq. ( 4.4 )) and the first-round load d / ( α c ​ M ) d/(\alpha_{c}M) . These axes control different effects. The parameter c c determines the statistical scale of the estimation error. For small c c , the post-failure d ^ − d \widehat{d}-d is dominated by the ± 2 \pm 2 offsets of a few duplicate edge pairs. For large c c , it approaches a continuous distribution. The load determines the position relative to the peeling phase transition: subcritical below 0.95, near the critical load from 0.95 to 1.05, and overloaded above 1.05. For fixed k , M k,M , the axes satisfy d / ( α c ​ M ) = c / ( α c ​ M ) d/(\alpha_{c}M)=c/(\alpha_{c}\sqrt{M}) . Thus, changing M M is necessary to vary the load while keeping c c fixed and separating the two effects. The statistical experiments use k = 3 , 4 , 5 k=3,4,5 and M ∈ { 256 , 1024 , 4096 , 16384 } M\in\{256,1024,4096,16384\} . For each pair ( k , M ) (k,M) , d d ranges over the union of three sets: the 8 values corresponding to c ∈ { 0.5 , 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 , 64 } c\in\{0.5,1,2,4,8,16,32,64\} , the 5 values corresponding to load ∈ { 0.95 , 1 , 1.05 , 1.5 , 3 } \in\{0.95,1,1.05,1.5,3\} , and the small differences d = 2 , 3 , 6 d=2,3,6 . Excluding loads above 3 leaves 189 configurations, with about 20,000 failures collected for each. Applying the same rule at M = 64 M=64 gives 42 configurations, which we use separately to test the rules’ limits of applicability. Figure H.1 in the appendix shows the configurations on both axes.

sections.heading: Planted sampling.
sections.text: We obtain failure samples by direct sampling or planted sampling, depending on the load. Near or above the critical load, failure is common. We generate random mappings and retain failures, obtaining samples from the true failure-conditioned distribution. At low load, the failure probability is small and direct sampling is too costly. By Proposition 2.1 , when d = o ⁡ ( M ) d=o(M) , failure is almost always caused by a pair of keys with identical mappings. We can construct such samples directly: choose a random pair of difference keys to share the same set of k k cells, then draw the mappings and signs of the remaining keys independently. We use direct sampling for the 84 statistical configurations with high failure rates and planted sampling for the remaining 105. The figures distinguish the two sampling methods (Appendix H.2 ). The planted-sampling control ( Exp-PLANT ) compares the two sample types on 12 planted configurations where direct sampling remains affordable. Among directly sampled failures, the fraction caused by a duplicate edge pair ranges from 0.988 to 1.000. The KS distance for X X ranges from 0.0048 to 0.0079, comparable to sampling error at this sample size, and the Skellam rule’s miss/u values also agree. The planted approximation deviates only near the critical load at small M M . The planted configurations in the statistical experiments lie outside this region (Appendix H.3 ).

sections.heading: 6.2 Random-sign encoding removes dependence on sign composition
sections.text: We verify two properties of random-sign encoding: the post-failure estimate is independent of sign composition, and decoding gives exactly the same result as the standard encoding.

sections.heading: Conditional bias.
sections.text: Under random-sign encoding, the post-failure d ^ \widehat{d} is unbiased for every sign composition. Under the standard encoding, conditioning the mapping on failure introduces a bias in d ^ \widehat{d} that depends on sign composition. Figure 6.1 compares three conditions on the same batch of 4 million mappings, with identical peeling outcomes in each trial. Under the standard encoding with a one-sided difference, the failure samples shift right, with mean + 0.599 +0.599 and KS distance 0.242 0.242 from all samples (Figure 6.1 (a)). With a balanced difference, the failure samples and all samples almost coincide (Figure 6.1 (b)). Under random-sign encoding, the failure samples have mean + 0.001 +0.001 and KS distance 0.001 0.001 , almost coinciding with all samples and N ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) N(0,1) (Figure 6.1 (c)). Figure 6.1: X = ( d ^ − d ) / s ⁡ ( d ) X=(\widehat{d}-d)/s(d) under three conditions on the same batch of mappings ( k = 3 k=3 , M = 16384 M=16384 , d = 13314 d=13314 , failure rate 0.125). (a)(b) Standard encoding with one-sided and balanced differences; (c) random-sign encoding. The dashed curve is N ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) N(0,1) . The standard encoding’s bias depends on both sign composition and k k . The horizontal axis in Figure 6.2 (a) covers five sign compositions, with d − / d d_{-}/d ranging from 0 0 (one-sided) to 0.5 0.5 (balanced). The solid lines for the standard encoding are near zero at the balanced point and deviate further as the difference becomes more one-sided. The direction depends on k k : for a one-sided difference, the bias is + 0.638 +0.638 at k = 3 k=3 and − 0.387 -0.387 at k = 6 k=6 (mechanism in Appendix B ). The receiver knows k k and hence the direction of the bias. Determining the correction’s magnitude also requires ( d + , d − ) (d_{+},d_{-}) , which is unknown in advance. The dashed lines for random-sign encoding remain near zero. Even with the vertical axis magnified about 40 times (Figure 6.2 (b)), the five sign compositions show no discernible difference. This agrees with Proposition 3.2 : the coding coefficients s i ​ ε i s_{i}\varepsilon_{i} are iid random signs with a distribution independent of ( d + , d − ) (d_{+},d_{-}) . The 84 direct-sampling configurations in the statistical experiments give the same conclusion (Appendix H.5 ). Figure 6.2: Mean post-failure X X versus sign composition ( M = 16384 M=16384 , failure probability about 0.1; both encodings share the same mappings for each configuration). The horizontal positions d − / d = 0 d_{-}/d=0 and 0.5 0.5 correspond to one-sided and balanced differences, respectively. Color indicates k k . (a) Standard encoding: solid lines and filled markers. Random-sign encoding: dashed lines and open markers. (b) Random-sign data from (a), with the vertical axis magnified about 40 times and error bars of two standard errors.

sections.heading: Decoding equivalence.
sections.text: Random-sign encoding preserves the set of keys recovered by decoding (Proposition 3.1 ) and therefore inherits the standard IBLT’s threshold and failure probability. The decoding-equivalence test ( Exp-DEC ) verifies this in paired trials on a complete IBLT. Both encodings share the same keys and cell hash. Each trial checks the first-round outcome, every accepted key, and the final recovered set against an independent degree-one peeling reference. We observe zero disagreements in more than 500 million paired trials (Appendix H.4 ). Table 6.1 reports failure probabilities near the threshold. After normalizing the load by the respective α c \alpha_{c} , the curves for the five values of k k almost coincide. The transition band narrows as M M grows, consistent with the critical window of width of order M − 1 / 2 M^{-1/2} in Section 2 . Table 6.1: First-round decoding failure probability. Columns give the load d / ( α c ​ M ) d/(\alpha_{c}M) . Both encodings agree in every trial, so the values apply to both. M = 1024 M=1024 M = 16384 M=16384 M = 65536 M=65536 k k α c \alpha_{c} 0.98 1 1.02 0.98 1 1.02 0.98 1 1.02 3 0.818 0.298 0.715 0.958 0.000 0.648 1.000 0.000 0.619 1.000 4 0.772 0.266 0.743 0.977 0.000 0.654 1.000 0.000 0.620 1.000 5 0.702 0.268 0.756 0.975 0.000 0.661 1.000 0.000 0.629 1.000 6 0.637 0.284 0.740 0.971 0.000 0.665 1.000 0.000 0.627 1.000 10 0.461 0.383 0.759 0.966 0.000 0.663 1.000 0.000 0.630 1.000 Proposition 3.1 assumes that the checksum makes no errors. In actual decoding, the checksum must reject cells of degree greater than one with count ± 1 \pm 1 . Random-sign encoding produces such cells even with one-sided differences: a degree-three cell with coding coefficients + 1 , + 1 , − 1 +1,+1,-1 has count + 1 +1 . All such candidates are rejected at the checksum step, with zero false acceptances. Their frequency under random-sign encoding is independent of sign composition and equals that under standard encoding with a balanced difference (Figure H.3 in the appendix). Section 6.6 reports the resulting additional decoding time.

sections.heading: 6.3 The discrete limit distribution accurately describes the post-failure lower tail at finite size
sections.text: The discrete limit distribution G d G_{d} coincides with the empirical post-failure lower tail without fitting, allowing the finite-size risk of both rules to be read directly from the figure. Figure 6.3 uses six configurations with c c ranging from 0.25 to 8 at k = 3 k=3 , M = 16384 M=16384 . It shows the empirical CDF of post-failure ( d ~ − d ) / s ⁡ ( d ) (\widetilde{d}-d)/s(d) (orange), G d G_{d} from Theorem 5.3 (black), and N ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) N(0,1) (dashed), on a logarithmic vertical axis to display the lower tail. We first examine the shape and then the risks of the two rules. Figure 6.3: Post-failure lower tail of ( d ~ − d ) / s ⁡ ( d ) (\widetilde{d}-d)/s(d) at different c c ( k = 3 k=3 , M = 16384 M=16384 ; 400,000 planted samples per configuration for c = 1 , 2 , 4 c=1,2,4 , and 100,000 for the rest). Below each title are the KS distances from the empirical CDF to G d G_{d} and to N ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) N(0,1) . The blue horizontal line marks CDF u = 0.01 u=0.01 ; the blue dotted vertical line sits at the 1% quantile − 2.33 -2.33 of N ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) N(0,1) and ends at the empirical CDF there.

sections.heading: Lower-tail shape.
sections.text: The black and orange curves almost coincide in all six configurations, with KS distances from the empirical CDF to G d G_{d} of 0.003–0.005. The quantiles of G d G_{d} thus match the true post-failure quantiles. The lower tail changes with c c : at small c c , it has only a few coarse steps; as c c grows, the steps become denser and approach the dashed curve. The steps arise from duplicate edge pairs. At small c c , failure is almost always caused by one such pair. If the edges have opposite signs, the observation is 2 below d d . This − 2 -2 offset is large relative to s ⁡ ( d ) s(d) : at c = 0.25 c=0.25 , it lies at a standardized error of about − 5.7 -5.7 , and about four tenths of the failure samples fall on this step, visible as the large step in the c = 0.25 c=0.25 panel. As c c grows, overlap among the remaining edges contributes many ± 2 / k \pm 2/k offsets that fill in the steps (Appendix H.6 ). The KS distance to N ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) N(0,1) drops from 0.496 at c = 0.25 c=0.25 to 0.015 at c = 8 c=8 . Finite-size error decreases as M M grows: across k = 3 , 4 , 5 k=3,4,5 , the KS distance to G d G_{d} at c = 1 , 2 , 4 c=1,2,4 drops from at most 0.034 at M = 256 M=256 to at most 0.012 at M = 16384 M=16384 (Table H.5 in the appendix).

sections.heading: Risk of the two rules.
sections.text: The horizontal line marks CDF u = 0.01 u=0.01 . The horizontal coordinate where a curve meets it is that distribution’s u u quantile. On this scale, the Gaussian rule’s acceptance lower bound Eq. ( 4.6 ) is approximately the u u quantile of N ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) N(0,1) , or − 2.33 -2.33 , where the dashed curve meets the horizontal line. A standardized error below this value causes rejection of the true d d . The height of the orange curve at − 2.33 -2.33 , marked by the top of the dotted vertical line, therefore approximates the Gaussian rule’s conditional miss rate. At c = 8 c=8 , all three curves meet the horizontal line at the same point, and the conditional miss rate is about 1.1 ​ u 1.1u . At c = 1 c=1 , the orange curve has height about 0.11 at − 2.33 -2.33 , or 11 ​ u 11u . At c = 0.25 c=0.25 , − 2.33 -2.33 lies to the right of the large step at − 5.7 -5.7 , and the orange curve has height about 0.49: roughly half the failure samples lead to underestimation. These readings agree with the miss/u values measured in the statistical experiments ( Exp-STAT ) in Section 6.4 (Table H.7 in the appendix). For candidate d d , the Skellam rule uses the black curve as its null distribution. Its rejection region is determined by the intersection of the black curve and the horizontal line, placing the risk near u u . At small c c , the horizontal line often crosses a vertical segment between two steps. The rule can reject only observations on the lower step and below, giving risk below u u and explaining its conservatism at small c c . Section 6.4 tests both observations across all 189 configurations.

sections.heading: 6.4 Conditional miss rate and extra capacity at finite size
sections.text: We test both rules’ risk at finite table sizes and measure the extra capacity required by the upper bound. Theorem 5.6 guarantees that the Skellam rule’s conditional miss rate is asymptotically at most u u for all d ≥ 2 d\geq 2 . The Gaussian rule has the same guarantee only when c → ∞ c\to\infty (Corollary 4.4 ). The conditional miss rate is the fraction of failure samples with a miss ( U < d U<d ), reported as miss/ u u . Values at most 1 indicate risk within the target. Extra capacity is ( U − d ) / d (U-d)/d . We first examine all configurations in Figure 6.4 , then retest those closest to the risk upper bound in Figure 6.5 .

sections.heading: Conditional miss rate.
sections.text: Figure 6.4 reports miss/u for all 189 configurations of the statistical experiments ( Exp-STAT ). The columns correspond to the two values of u u ; the top and bottom rows use direct and planted sampling, respectively. At very small c c , failure is so rare that only planted sampling supplies samples (Section 6.1 ). The circles for the Skellam rule lie near the dashed line miss/u = 1 =1 when c ≥ 8 c\geq 8 and fall below it as c c decreases. Values near 1 indicate that the rule uses the risk budget without exceeding it: the maximum is 1.04, while with about 20,000 failures per configuration, the standard error of miss/u at u = 0.01 u=0.01 is about 0.07. Values below 1 result from the steps in Figure 6.3 : when u u falls between two steps, the rule can reject only the lower step and below, giving risk below u u . This is especially visible at u = 0.01 u=0.01 , where circles in the bottom row lie on the lower boundary, indicating zero misses. Figure 6.4: miss/u versus c = d / M c=d/\sqrt{M} in the statistical experiments ( k = 3 , 4 , 5 k=3,4,5 , M = 256 M=256 –16384, about 20,000 failures per configuration; configurations with zero misses appear on the lower boundary). Top: direct sampling. Bottom: planted sampling. Circles: Skellam rule. Triangles: Gaussian rule. Figure 6.5: Estimated miss/u for the Skellam rule with two-sided 95% intervals (Clopper–Pearson) on the Exp-WORST configurations. Configurations are ordered by load, shown in parentheses. The dashed line marks miss/u = 1 =1 . The triangles for the Gaussian rule coincide with the circles only when c ≥ 8 c\geq 8 and rise rapidly as c c decreases. At u = 0.01 u=0.01 , miss/u is about 8–11 at c = 1 c=1 and exceeds 33 at c = 0.5 c=0.5 (Table H.7 in the appendix). In the bottom row, most triangles with c < 0.3 c<0.3 form a horizontal line: the miss rate stays at 1 / 2 1/2 , or miss/u = 1 / ( 2 ​ u ) =1/(2u) , giving 50 and 10 in the two columns. At very small c c , the post-failure observation falls near d + 2 d+2 or d − 2 d-2 with probability one half each (Proposition F.1 ). The latter lies to the left of the Gaussian quantile, as illustrated by the large step at c = 0.25 c=0.25 in Figure 6.3 . The few triangles on the lower boundary correspond to d = 2 , 3 d=2,3 : the observation is then below the acceptance thresholds of all candidates, so the Gaussian rule returns + ∞ +\infty . This excess risk persists as table size grows, consistent with the finite limit in Theorem 5.3 .

sections.heading: Worst-configuration retest.
sections.text: About 20,000 failures per configuration in Figure 6.4 are insufficient to confirm that configurations closest to the risk upper bound also meet the target. The worst-configuration test ( Exp-WORST ) selects 12 such configurations using a rule fixed before sampling, covering bounded c c , the critical window, and overload. Independent samples provide 56,000 to 330,000 failures per configuration. Figure 6.5 orders these configurations by load from top to bottom. All 24 estimates are at most 0.99, and 22 two-sided 95% intervals lie entirely to the left of 1. The largest one-sided simultaneous confidence upper bound is 1.024 ​ u 1.024u , meeting the 1.1 ​ u 1.1u criterion set before sampling (Appendix H.7 ). The lowest-load configuration at u = 0.01 u=0.01 lies farthest from 1, consistent with the conservatism at small c c in Figure 6.4 .

sections.heading: Extra capacity.
sections.text: Controlling misses requires an upper bound above d d . When c ≥ 8 c\geq 8 , extra capacity is determined by table size and decreases as M − 1 / 2 M^{-1/2} , with nearly identical values for both rules: U − d U-d is about 2.3–2.8 times s ⁡ ( d ) s(d) and s ⁡ ( d ) / d ≈ 2 / M s(d)/d\approx\sqrt{2/M} . At u = 0.01 u=0.01 , the Skellam rule’s median extra capacity drops from 25% at M = 256 M=256 to 2.6% at M = 16384 M=16384 (Table H.6 in the appendix). When c c is bounded, d d itself is small, making the ratio less informative, and few extra elements are needed: at c = 4 c=4 , the median U − d U-d is 15. In the two-round protocol, this extra capacity appears as the increase in second-round table size over the oracle (Section 6.5 ). We recommend M ≥ 1024 M\geq 1024 for deployment. The null distribution in Section 5 omits cells shared by the duplicate edge pair and the remaining keys. Its occurrence rate, ( d − 2 ) ​ k 2 / M (d-2)k^{2}/M , grows as table size decreases. At M = 64 M=64 , this omission becomes nonnegligible: the Skellam rule’s maximum miss/u is 1.08, beyond sampling error. At M = 256 M=256 , we observe no excess in miss/u beyond sampling error. At the same c c , the omitted structure is more frequent than at M = 1024 M=1024 , and median extra capacity reaches 25%.

sections.heading: 6.5 The two-round protocol on a complete IBLT
sections.text: Theorem 5.7 decomposes the two-round failure probability into two core risks, the joint miss rate and peeling failure with sufficient capacity, and two additional risks, an infinite upper bound and checksum error. We run the two-round protocol on a complete IBLT to compare the first two terms in practice, measure the random-sign IBLT’s communication cost, and compare it with the existing calibration rule. The protocol experiments ( Exp-PROTO ) use k = 3 , 4 , 5 k=3,4,5 , first-round table sizes M 1 ∈ { 256 , 1024 , 4096 , 16384 } M_{1}\in\{256,1024,4096,16384\} , and first-round loads 0.95, 1, 1.05, 1.5, 3. We test two sign compositions, one-sided (all on the A A side) and balanced, for a total of 120 configurations. The two sides also hold 1000 common elements. We fix each configuration’s trial count in advance using a pilot estimate of the first-round failure probability. We target about 20,000 first-round failures, capped at 3,000,000 trials. Configurations with no first-round failure in the pilot receive a fixed 100,000 trials. Both values of u u use the same trials. After each first-round failure, we run the second round separately with table sizes determined by three upper bounds: the Skellam rule, the Gaussian rule, and an oracle using the true d d . Both rules use U b = max ⁡ ( U , | b | ) U_{b}=\max(U,|b|) as in Section 3.2 . The second-round table size is max ⁡ { ⌈ U b / ( 0.8 ​ α c ) ⌉ , 64 } \max\{\lceil U_{b}/(0.8\alpha_{c})\rceil,64\} , with a fresh cell hash. All three upper bounds share the keys and hashes within each trial, allowing paired comparisons that differ only in the upper bound (implementation details in Appendix H.8 ). The two-round protocol achieves reliability comparable to the oracle. In Figure 6.6 (a), both rules’ final failure rates fall in the same range as the oracle’s, all at most 0.13% when M 1 ≥ 1024 M_{1}\geq 1024 . At u = 0.01 u=0.01 , their maximum is at most the oracle’s (Table H.9 in the appendix). In paired comparisons by configuration, only the configuration used in the example of Section 5.5 has a 95% paired interval excluding zero: the Skellam rule has 10 final failures and the Gaussian rule has 20. Final failures arise mainly from second-round peeling, consistent with the expected dominance of the second term in Theorem 5.7 . At u = 0.01 u=0.01 , after pooling configurations by M 1 M_{1} , at most 6% of final failures follow a miss. The second-round table size includes a margin of 1 / ( 0.8 ​ α c ) 1/(0.8\alpha_{c}) , which absorbs most slight underestimates. This margin also explains why the rules perform at least as well as the oracle: their upper bounds usually exceed d d , yielding slightly larger second-round tables and fewer peeling failures. Extra communication cost depends only on M 1 M_{1} and decreases as M 1 − 1 / 2 M_{1}^{-1/2} . In Figure 6.6 (b), configurations with different k k , loads, and sign compositions almost coincide at each M 1 M_{1} and follow the dotted line with slope − 1 / 2 -1/2 . At u = 0.01 u=0.01 , the Skellam rule’s increase in second-round table size over the oracle drops from 25.6% at M 1 = 256 M_{1}=256 to 2.6% at M 1 = 16384 M_{1}=16384 , consistent with the extra capacity in Section 6.4 . In total bytes, the overhead drops from 14.6% to 1.5%. Figure 6.6: Two-round protocol as first-round table size M 1 M_{1} varies (120 configurations, 13.94 million trials per u u ). (a) Final two-round failure rate for each configuration at u = 0.01 u=0.01 . Configurations with zero failures appear at 0 below the axis break. (b) Increase in second-round table size over the oracle after first-round failure, with one point per configuration. The dotted line has slope − 1 / 2 -1/2 . Figure 6.7 shows the same trend at fixed load (first-round target load 1.5, balanced, u = 0.01 u=0.01 ). As table size grows, the Skellam rule’s miss/u approaches 1 from below, while the Gaussian rule stays near 1. Each point in the top row pools all first-round failures for one configuration (Appendix H.7 ). Total byte overhead relative to the oracle drops from 16.8% at M 1 = 256 M_{1}=256 to 1.7% at M 1 = 16384 M_{1}=16384 and becomes negligible as table size grows. Figure 6.7: Two-round protocol at fixed load as table size varies (balanced, u = 0.01 u=0.01 , target load 1.5). Each column corresponds to one k k . Top: all first-round failures pooled by configuration (331,000 to 372,000 per point). Bottom: communication overhead relative to the oracle for the same configuration.

sections.heading: Comparison with the existing calibration rule.
sections.text: Prior work [ 32 ] also sets second-round capacity from the post-failure d ^ \widehat{d} in a standard IBLT. Because the post-failure bias depends on the unknown sign composition, it obtains a calibration factor from offline simulation. For k = 3 k=3 , it groups configurations by first-round table size and takes the worst post-failure 1% quantile q 0.01 q_{0.01} of d ^ / d \widehat{d}/d over several loads and sign compositions, then sets U = ⌈ d ^ / q 0.01 ⌉ U=\lceil\widehat{d}/q_{0.01}\rceil . We use this upper bound in the same protocol, keeping all other settings identical to those for our two rules; Table H.10 in the appendix gives the complete results. Two findings emerge. First, under standard encoding, the risk of the same factor varies widely with sign composition: at loads 0.95–1.0, conditional miss rates are 0.05 0.05 – 0.40 ​ u 0.40u for one-sided differences and 0.86 0.86 – 0.94 ​ u 0.94u for balanced differences, an order-of-magnitude difference. This is the protocol-level consequence of the bias in Section 6.2 , and the factor must be calibrated for the worst sign composition. Random-sign encoding brings both into 0.80 0.80 – 1.01 ​ u 1.01u . Second, the factor requires separate simulation calibration for each parameter configuration. The published values cover only k = 3 k=3 , M 1 ≤ 4096 M_{1}\leq 4096 , and u = 0.01 u=0.01 . For these parameters, the calibration rule and the Skellam rule have similar final failure rates and total byte costs. We compute the Skellam rule directly from the theoretical distribution in Section 5 , without calibration for any k k , M M , load, or u u .

sections.heading: 6.6 Computational cost and rule choice
sections.text: Almost all computation beyond standard encoding comes from sizing with the Skellam rule. The overhead of random-sign encoding itself is negligible. With random-sign encoding, the decoder processes every difference as a balanced difference: cells containing multiple keys with count ± 1 \pm 1 also enter the candidate queue and are then rejected by the checksum. For a one-sided difference, the number of candidates checked per recovered key therefore rises from 1.00 to 1.77 ( k = 3 k=3 ). The resulting increase in decoding time is 1–2% of total protocol time at loads 1.0–1.05 and less than 1% at higher loads. In deployment, sizing with the Skellam rule requires only a table lookup. The parameters ( M 1 , k , u ) (M_{1},k,u) are fixed, and U U depends only on the single observed integer ∑ v C v 2 \sum_{v}C_{v}^{2} . We can therefore precompute U U for each possible observation within a chosen range and store the results in a table indexed by the observation. After computing ∑ v C v 2 \sum_{v}C_{v}^{2} , the receiver retrieves U U directly. The results agree entry by entry with online computation (Appendix G.5 ). Table 6.2 reports total protocol time at M 1 = 16384 M_{1}=16384 , including first-round encoding and decoding, sizing, and the second round. With table lookup, each sizing takes less than 1 μ \mu s, and total protocol time differs from the Gaussian rule by less than 0.5%. When parameters vary across synchronizations, precomputation is inconvenient, or the observation exceeds the table’s range, the Skellam rule computes the upper bound online. Online computation evaluates the exact CDF for each candidate, with cost growing roughly as c 2 c^{2} . Total protocol time is 15–24% longer than for the Gaussian rule at loads 1.0–1.05 and 40–45% longer at load 1.5. At load 3, sizing dominates, and total time is 3.1–3.8 times that of the Gaussian rule. A receiver can cache Poisson probability tables across synchronizations to reduce this cost. Appendix H.9 gives the conditions for the computational-cost measurement ( Exp-COST ), table construction and verification, and per-sizing time and memory use under different cache conditions.
