Lookup and online are two implementations of the Skellam rule; the online implementation caches Poisson probability tables between successive trials. Skellam rule (lookup) Skellam rule (online) Gaussian rule Load k = 3 k=3 k = 4 k=4 k = 5 k=5 k = 3 k=3 k = 4 k=4 k = 5 k=5 k = 3 k=3 k = 4 k=4 k = 5 k=5 1.0 11.0 14.0 15.3 12.7 16.8 17.7 11.0 14.0 15.3 1.05 13.1 15.6 18.2 16.2 19.4 21.5 13.1 15.6 18.2 1.5 14.0 16.7 19.6 20.1 24.2 27.6 14.0 16.7 19.6 3 18.9 22.4 25.7 58.8 85.4 90.1 18.8 22.3 25.6 The Gaussian rule meets the target only when d ≫ M d\gg\sqrt{M} . Table size alone does not exclude bounded c c or fixed small d d , so the rule is suitable only for applications whose workloads ensure this condition. The Skellam rule applies to all d ≥ 2 d\geq 2 without knowing the load region, and with table lookup its sizing cost is no higher than that of the Gaussian rule. For deployment, we recommend the Skellam rule with M 1 ≥ 1024 M_{1}\geq 1024 (Section 6.4 ).

sections.heading: IBLT and set reconciliation.
sections.text: IBLT [ 17 ] and the invertible Bloom filter [ 13 ] list set differences by peeling. Decoding success is determined by the 2-core of a random hypergraph [ 26 , 12 , 11 ] . At low load, duplicate edge pairs dominate failure [ 17 , 34 ] , and the probability of a linear-sized core at subcritical load is exponentially small [ 21 , 10 ] . Subsequent work improves the hypergraph structure [ 23 ] , develops rateless codes [ 33 , 24 ] , adds a stash to lower the failure probability [ 4 ] , or predicts and breaks the 2-core after decoding failure [ 15 ] . These works seek to reduce failure or resume decoding after failure. We read the same table after failure to determine the next-round capacity.

sections.heading: Estimating the difference size.
sections.text: A common approach to estimating d d is to send a separate estimator, such as the strata estimator [ 13 ] , min-wise hashing [ 6 ] , the odd sketch [ 25 ] , or GXBits [ 20 ] . PBS [ 16 ] first estimates d d using independent ToW sketches, then sets capacity to a fixed multiple of the estimate. It transmits and accounts for the estimator and reconciliation structure separately. We obtain the estimate from the same counts used for decoding, avoiding a separate estimator. This reuse requires analysis conditional on decoding failure: the estimate is needed only after failure, and failure selects the mapping.

sections.heading: Random-sign sketches and second-moment estimation.
sections.text: AMS [ 1 ] estimates F 2 F_{2} using a sum of random signs. CountSketch [ 7 ] supports point queries with random-sign counters. Thorup and Zhang [ 30 ] analyze its second-moment extension and give a centered second-moment estimate for a single counter array. Fast-AGMS [ 9 ] uses the same structure for distributed queries. d ^ \widehat{d} has the same algebraic form as these estimators. Its conditional unbiasedness given the mapping also follows the structure of the Hutchinson trace estimator [ 18 ] . These sketches carry no decodable keySum and do not address the distribution conditional on decoding failure. Fischer and Nakos [ 14 ] combine hypergraph peeling and a random-sign CountSketch in a single linear sketch, with the tail norm estimated by a separate short sketch. We encode the shared random signs in the IBLT’s count, keySum, and checksum. The same table supports peeling and, after failure, provides an estimate independent of the difference direction, together with a post-failure upper bound valid at all loads.

sections.heading: Reading the same table after failure.
sections.text: Prior work [ 32 ] reads count energy after first-round failure to set the second-round capacity. Its analysis models sign composition with iid signs and obtains a conditional mean equal to d d . Its upper-bound rule uses a chi-square approximation under deep overload and per-configuration simulation calibration at other loads, where its analytic bound is too conservative for small M M . We encode random signs in all three IBLT fields, making these properties hold exactly for every fixed mapping. We also derive a post-failure distribution and upper bound valid at all loads.

sections.heading: Conditional limits and discrete approximations.
sections.text: For bounded c c (Eq. ( 4.4 )), we derive the limit distribution using the Chen–Stein method [ 2 ] for the Poisson approximation of sparse overlap. The Skellam distribution describes the difference between two types of counts. At low load, we replace the failure-conditioned distribution with the planted distribution, which is the distribution size-biased by the duplicate edge pair count [ 3 ] . When d ≫ M d\gg\sqrt{M} , we analyze the random-sign quadratic form given the mapping using the cumulant method on a dependency graph [ 19 ] . This requires only concentration bounds [ 31 , 8 ] and degree control for the overlap graph. We prove a Gaussian limit uniform over deterministic coefficients using an edge-exposure martingale CLT. The upper-bound rule uses classical test inversion [ 27 ] .

sections.heading: 8 Discussion and conclusion
sections.text: The random-sign IBLT uses a single table for both decoding and difference-size estimation, preserving the cells and decoding capability. The mapping alone determines decoding success, while the signs supply the estimate’s randomness. This separation makes the estimate exactly unbiased for every fixed mapping and identically distributed across sign compositions. It also lets us fully characterize the post-failure distribution: Gaussian when d ≫ M d\gg\sqrt{M} , and discrete with a ± 2 \pm 2 term plus a Skellam term when c = d / M c=d/\sqrt{M} is bounded. One family of distributions describes all scales. Using this family as the null distribution, the Skellam rule keeps the conditional miss rate asymptotically at most the target risk, uniformly over all d ≥ 2 d\geq 2 . For deployment, we recommend the Skellam rule, which retains the uniform guarantee for all d ≥ 2 d\geq 2 . When ( M 1 , k , u ) (M_{1},k,u) is fixed, its upper bounds can be precomputed and stored in a table, reducing sizing to a single lookup. Section 6.6 gives the guarantees and costs of the two rules. The Skellam rule meets the target within sampling error on all experimental configurations with M ≥ 256 M\geq 256 , and we recommend M ≥ 1024 M\geq 1024 for deployment (Section 6.4 ). Shortening the checksum to 32 bits yields narrower cells while preserving the sizing risk. The verification error probability is of order 10 − 4 10^{-4} at M 1 = 16384 M_{1}=16384 and load at most 3 (Section 5.5 ). Storing counts for several independent signs per cell reduces absolute error while preserving the ratio of the post-failure conditional scale to the unconditional scale. Inversion still uses the post-failure distribution (Appendix F.6 ). Random-sign encoding preserves cell space overhead, and the additional decoding time is at most about 2% of total protocol time (Section 6.6 ). Three questions remain for future work. First, rigorous finite-parameter tail upper bounds could reject more candidates before constructing the Poisson tables, reducing the Skellam rule’s computational cost. Second, making the error constants in Theorem 5.3 and Theorem 4.2 computable would give a finite risk bound for a specified M M . Third, we seek to extend the method to multiset differences whose weights can exceed one. In this setting, the random-sign count gives an unbiased estimate of the difference vector’s F 2 F_{2} . Decoding and post-failure analysis for this extension remain to be developed.

In the standard IBLT, the count is C v = ∑ i : v ∈ S i s i C_{v}=\sum_{i:v\in S_{i}}s_{i} , with the set direction as the coefficient. sections.heading: Appendix C Encoding properties and proofs of exact moments
sections.text: We describe the XOR implementation of keySum and checksum and prove the finite identities in Sections 3 and 4 . We then summarize their exact verification for small parameter values and discuss the AMS observation obtained from the count sum.

sections.heading: C.1 XOR implementation
sections.text: In the set model, each side inserts each key at most once. We can therefore accumulate keySum and checksum by bitwise XOR, as in a common implementation of the standard IBLT, and multiply only the count by ε ⁡ ( x ) \varepsilon(x) . Under XOR, − x = x -x=x . Thus, in each difference-table cell, keySum is the XOR of the differing keys that select the cell, and checksum is the XOR of their chk \mathrm{chk} values. Both are independent of the coding coefficients. In a pure cell, keySum and checksum equal x i x_{i} and chk ⁡ ( x i ) \mathrm{chk}(x_{i}) directly, so we check whether checksum equals chk ⁡ ( x ) \mathrm{chk}(x) . To delete x i x_{i} , we subtract C v C_{v} from the count and XOR the other two fields once more with x i x_{i} and chk ⁡ ( x i ) \mathrm{chk}(x_{i}) , respectively. The induction argument for the additive form in the next subsection also applies here. We recover the direction as C v ​ ε ​ ( x ) C_{v}\,\varepsilon(x) , and peeling follows the same process and gives the same result as in the additive form. In a multiset, the same key may be inserted repeatedly. XOR cancels repeated contributions while the count retains them, so multisets require the additive form. If peeling modifies the difference table in place, the receiver can accumulate the two scalars ∑ v C v 2 \sum_{v}C_{v}^{2} and ∑ v C v \sum_{v}C_{v} during cell-by-cell subtraction, without retaining the original difference table.

sections.heading: C.2 Proof of Proposition 3.1 (ideal decoding equivalence)
sections.text: Proof. We induct on the number of peeling steps. After each step, the three fields of every cell equal the encoded sum of the remaining keys: the count is ∑ s i ​ ε i \sum s_{i}\varepsilon_{i} , keySum is ∑ s i ​ ε i ​ x i \sum s_{i}\varepsilon_{i}x_{i} , and checksum is ∑ s i ​ ε i ​ chk ​ ( x i ) \sum s_{i}\varepsilon_{i}\,\mathrm{chk}(x_{i}) . Each sum ranges over the remaining keys that select the cell. This invariant holds initially by Eq. ( 3.1 ). Suppose that at some step cell v v has degree one in the unsigned hypergraph, with unique key x i x_{i} . Its count is s i ​ ε i ∈ { ± 1 } s_{i}\varepsilon_{i}\in\{\pm 1\} , count times keySum equals x i x_{i} , and checksum equals count times chk ⁡ ( x i ) \mathrm{chk}(x_{i}) . The cell hash of x i x_{i} also contains v v , so v v passes the pure-cell test. Conversely, a cell of any other degree that passes the test is a false positive, which the ideal-purity assumption excludes. Thus the cells removable under random-sign encoding are exactly the unsigned degree-one cells. To delete x i x_{i} , we subtract its three-field contribution multiplied by the coding coefficient s i ​ ε i s_{i}\varepsilon_{i} from its k k cells. This preserves the invariant and removes the corresponding edge from the unsigned hypergraph. With the same cell-selection order, the two processes reach the same endpoint. Peeling always ends at the 2-core, independently of the selection order, so F F depends only on 𝒢 \mathcal{G} . At termination, we check all fields. Under random signs, a nonempty core can have all-zero counts, so counts alone cannot certify success. The keySum fields can cancel at the same time. Success is misjudged only if all checksums are also zero. This event is included in E E in Section 5.5 . ∎

sections.heading: D.2 Failure structure at fixed subcritical load
sections.text: Lemma D.3 (Fixed subcritical load) . Let d / M → α ∈ ( 0 , α c ) d/M\to\alpha\in(0,\alpha_{c}) . Then Pr ( F ∖ { | core | = 2 } ) = O ( M − b k ) \Pr(F\setminus\{|\mathrm{core}|=2\})=O(M^{-b_{k}}) , Pr ⁡ ( F ) = μ ⁡ { 1 + O ⁡ ( M − δ k ) } \Pr(F)=\mu\{1+O(M^{-\delta_{k}})\} , and ‖ ℒ ⁡ ( 𝒢 ∣ F ) − Q ‖ T ​ V = O ⁡ ( M − δ k ) \|\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{G}\mid F)-Q\|_{TV}=O(M^{-\delta_{k}}) , where | core | |\mathrm{core}| is the number of edges of the 2-core and δ k = min ⁡ { k − 2 , b k − ( k − 2 ) } ≥ 1 \delta_{k}=\min\{k-2,\,b_{k}-(k-2)\}\geq 1 . For the binomial hypergraph H ⁡ ( n , p , k ) H(n,p;k) , Kim [ 21 ] , Theorem 1.7, proves that the probability that the 2-core has at least δ ​ n \delta n vertices is exponentially small at subcritical load. We follow the finite-round neighborhood analysis and concentration argument for LDPC codes [ 28 ] , treating cell degrees separately because they have no fixed upper bound in our model. sections.text: Lemma D.4 (Superpolynomial graph concentration) . Fix k ≥ 3 k\geq 3 , and let d / M d/M lie in a fixed compact interval of ( 0 , ∞ ) (0,\infty) . sections.text: Suppose each cell stores L L copies of the count, using independent sign hashes and a shared mapping. The reason is that for fixed small d d , failure is caused by a duplicate edge pair, which contributes ± 2 \pm 2 independently in each copy, while the acceptance lower bound tends to d d as s ⁡ ( d ) → 0 s(d)\to 0 . Increasing the number of copies therefore cannot replace the correct post-failure distribution, which is why the main text uses a single count with the discrete limit distribution.

sections.heading: Appendix G Exact evaluation and search cutoffs
sections.text: This appendix describes the computation of the Skellam rule (Definition 5.5 ). The guarantee of the Skellam rule does not require the accepted candidates to form an interval, and by definition U U is the largest accepted candidate. Rejected candidates may lie between accepted ones, so a binary search can miss the largest accepted candidate. The implementation therefore scans downward from an explicit cutoff and returns the first accepted candidate; under the condition of Proposition G.1 , the result equals that of an unbounded scan. Appendix G.1 evaluates G n ​ ( d ~ ) G_{n}(\widetilde{d}) exactly using integer thresholds; Appendix G.2 gives the cutoff and proves that every candidate above it is rejected; Appendices G.3 and G.4 give the per-candidate prescreening and the exact CDF computation; the comparisons confirm that none of these measures changes the output of the rule. Appendix G.5 explains how to precompute a table of U U when the parameters are fixed.

Prescreening only rejects candidates certified for rejection; disabling it and computing the exact CDF for every candidate gives the same result case by case.

sections.heading: G.4 Windowed Poisson table for the exact CDF
sections.text: We use Pr ⁡ ( Z n ≤ j ) = ∑ m Pr ⁡ ( P 2 = m ) ​ Pr ⁡ ( P 1 ≤ j + m ) \Pr(Z_{n}\leq j)=\sum_{m}\Pr(P_{2}=m)\Pr(P_{1}\leq j+m) , where P 1 , P 2 P_{1},P_{2} are independent Pois ⁡ ( λ n ) \operatorname{Pois}(\lambda_{n}) variables. By Eq. ( 5.3 ), λ n ≈ k 2 ​ n 2 / ( 4 ​ M ) \lambda_{n}\approx k^{2}n^{2}/(4M) grows quadratically with the candidate: at M 1 = 16384 M_{1}=16384 and load 3 3 , λ n \lambda_{n} ranges from about 2 × 10 5 2\times 10^{5} to 4 × 10 5 4\times 10^{5} . The initial implementation built the table from zero to λ n + 14 ​ λ n \lambda_{n}+14\sqrt{\lambda_{n}} ; a single sizing took about 1.3 1.3 s and exhausted memory in early two-round runs. The implementation therefore builds, for each candidate, a Poisson table restricted to the window centered at λ n \lambda_{n} with half-width 14 ​ λ n + 40 14\sqrt{\lambda_{n}}+40 : starting at the mode, we compute the pmf recursively in both directions using p ⁡ ( i + 1 ) = p ⁡ ( i ) ​ λ n / ( i + 1 ) p(i+1)=p(i)\lambda_{n}/(i+1) , normalize within the window, and accumulate the CDF. Substituting this half-width into the Chernoff bound for the two-sided Poisson tail gives an exponent of at least 98 98 for every λ n \lambda_{n} , so the mass beyond each end of the window is below 10 − 40 10^{-40} , smaller than double-precision rounding error; normalization also avoids the relative error from evaluating log ⁡ Γ \log\Gamma term by term at large λ n \lambda_{n} . The upper bounds before and after windowing agree case by case. Both the number of candidates requiring an exact CDF and the window length are proportional to c c , so the cost of a single sizing is roughly proportional to λ d \lambda_{d} ; Appendix H.9 reports measurements. The Poisson table depends only on ( M , k ) (M,k) and n n , so it can be shared across syncs and risk levels. The implementation maintains a cache keyed by ( M , k ) (M,k) . When full, it evicts the least recently used tables until half its capacity is free. Capacity is measured in entries, each containing two float64 values. Under the condition of Proposition G.1 , the cutoff, prescreening, and windowed tables preserve the output of the rule. We compare case by case against a reference implementation with 70 decimal digits of precision on 4536 general cases and 286 bounded- c c cases, covering lattice points, parity boundaries, and + ∞ +\infty . We also compare the windowed implementation with cutoffs against the full-table implementation on 9779 cases. The value M = 16 M=16 lies on both sides of the condition of Proposition G.1 : the rule returns + ∞ +\infty at u = 0.01 u=0.01 and a finite upper bound at u = 0.05 u=0.05 . On the 2406 cases with M = 16 M=16 , k = 3 , 4 , 5 k=3,4,5 , u = 0.01 , 0.05 u=0.01,0.05 , and R = 0 , … , 400 R=0,\dots,400 , we compare all three implementations. All three comparisons agree case by case.

sections.heading: G.5 Table lookup with fixed parameters
sections.text: When ( M , k , u ) (M,k,u) is fixed, U U depends only on the integer R R . We can precompute U U for every R R up to a chosen limit and store the results in a table indexed by R R . For a fixed candidate n n , both floors are nondecreasing in R R , so G n ​ ( d ~ ) G_{n}(\widetilde{d}) is nondecreasing in R R as well. The Chernoff bound used for prescreening is also nondecreasing in R R . Thus, the values of R R for which candidate n n is accepted form an integer interval unbounded above, whose left endpoint can be found by binary search. Recording each candidate at its left endpoint and then taking prefix maxima in increasing order of R R gives the largest accepted candidate, U U , at every R R in the table. Candidates need only be checked up to the cutoff at the table’s upper limit: the cutoff increases with R R , and every candidate above it is rejected at each R R in the table (Proposition G.1 ). Table lookup and the sequential search use the same acceptance test and agree entry by entry. Observations beyond the table are still computed online as described above. Appendix H.9 reports table sizes and construction times.

sections.heading: Appendix H Experimental setup and supplementary results
sections.text: This appendix gives the setup and supplementary results of the experiments in Section 6 .

sections.heading: H.1 Validation goals and experiment overview
sections.text: The experiments fall into four groups according to the conclusion they test, and the following subsections follow this order. Experiment tags identify them in the main text and appendix.

sections.heading: Source of failure samples.
sections.text: The statistical experiments ( Exp-STAT ) use the 189 configurations of Section 6.1 , plus 42 boundary configurations at M = 64 M=64 , with about 20,000 failures per configuration. Configurations with rare failures sample from the planted distribution in place of the failure-conditioned distribution (Lemma D.2 ). The planted sampling control ( Exp-PLANT ) tests the finite-size error of this substitution: the low-load group directly checks the planted samples used by the statistical experiments in 12 configurations, and the critical-load group uses 21 configurations with M = 64 M=64 to 1024 to locate the range of the approximation. Appendix H.2 and Appendix H.3 give the sampling method and the control results.

sections.heading: Properties of the random-sign encoding.
sections.text: Random-sign encoding preserves decoding (Proposition 3.1 ), and the decoding-equivalence test ( Exp-DEC ) verifies this on the full IBLT with more than 500 million paired trials, counting rejected candidates under both encodings (Appendix H.4 ). The post-failure estimate is conditionally unbiased for any sign composition (Propositions 4.1 and 3.2 ), and the conditional-unbiasedness test ( Exp-UNB ) verifies this on 203 configurations (Appendix H.5 ).

sections.heading: Lower-tail shape and conditional miss rate.
sections.text: The failure records of the statistical experiments ( Exp-STAT ) compare the post-failure lower tail with the discrete and Gaussian limits (Theorems 5.3 and 4.2 , Appendix H.6 ) and measure the conditional miss rate and extra capacity of the two rules at finite size (Theorem 5.6 and Corollary 4.4 , Appendix H.7 ). The worst-configuration test ( Exp-WORST ) uses independent samples to test the Skellam rule’s conditional miss rate on the 12 configurations closest to the risk bound, with 56,000 to 330,000 failures per configuration.

sections.heading: Two-round protocol and computation cost.
sections.text: The protocol experiments ( Exp-PROTO ) run the two-round protocol on a real IBLT over 120 configurations with M 1 = 256 M_{1}=256 to 16384, first-round load 0.95 to 3, and one-sided and balanced sign compositions, measuring reliability and communication cost (Theorem 5.7 , Appendix H.8 ). The computation-cost measurement ( Exp-COST ) gives the time and memory of sizing and decoding at M = 16384 M=16384 (Appendix H.9 ).

sections.heading: Design fixed before sampling.
sections.text: Before launch, we fix the configurations, seeds, sampling sources, stopping rules, and budgets for the statistical experiments ( Exp-STAT ), the worst-configuration test ( Exp-WORST ), the planted sampling control ( Exp-PLANT ), and the protocol experiments ( Exp-PROTO ) using a single feasibility pilot. We fix the selection rule for the worst-configuration test before the statistical experiments begin, then derive the specific configurations and sample sizes from that rule after the statistical experiments finish (Appendix H.7 ). The conditional-unbiasedness test ( Exp-UNB ) and the decoding-equivalence test ( Exp-DEC ) come from separate independent runs, and the computation-cost measurement ( Exp-COST ) is conducted outside the other runs (Appendix H.9 ).

sections.heading: H.2 Sampling method
sections.text: There are two sources of failure samples. Direct sampling generates mappings independently and runs peeling, retaining only the failure samples; obtaining one failure requires 1 / Pr ⁡ ( F ) 1/\Pr(F) mappings on average. Planted sampling picks a pair of difference keys uniformly at random, makes them share a uniformly random k k -cell set, generates the mappings of the remaining keys independently and uniformly, and draws the signs independently; this construction produces a peeling failure every time, and the resulting mapping follows Q Q . Under iid random signs the statistic is invariant under label permutation, so the implementation equivalently fixes the last two labels as the duplicate edge pair. Lemma D.2 gives the asymptotic relation between the planted distribution and the true failure-conditioned distribution, and Appendix H.3 compares them at finite size. The statistical experiments ( Exp-STAT ) choose between the two sources according to the cost estimated in the pilot: configurations whose 20,000 direct failures are expected to cost at most 20 CPU core-hours use direct sampling with ⌈ 2 × 10 4 / Pr ^ ​ ( F ) ⌉ \lceil 2\times 10^{4}/\widehat{\Pr}(F)\rceil trials, and the remaining configurations use 20,000 planted samples. Figure H.1 shows each configuration’s location in c c and load and its sampling source. The six points at load 3 ( d = round ⁡ ( 3 ​ α c ​ M ) d=\mathrm{round}(3\alpha_{c}M) , with rounding making the load slightly above 3) run separately with independent seeds after the statistical experiments finish, using the same sampling method and target failure count as the other configurations. Figure H.1: The 189 configurations of the statistical experiments. Point shapes indicate the sampling source. Vertical lines mark the grouping boundaries of c c , and horizontal shading marks load 0.95–1.05. All 203 configurations of the conditional-unbiasedness test ( Exp-UNB ) use direct sampling on CPUs with sequential peeling, with table sizes up to M = 262144 M=262144 .

sections.heading: H.3 Finite-size error of the planted distribution
sections.text: The planted sampling control ( Exp-PLANT ) tests whether the planted samples used in the main text can replace direct failure samples. The conclusion has two parts: in the low-load region where the statistical experiments actually use planted samples, the two samples show no detectable difference; near the critical load, the planted approximation still holds at M = 1024 M=1024 and degrades as M M decreases, with the planted sample giving higher miss at M = 64 M=64 .

sections.heading: Compared quantities and criteria.
sections.text: Each configuration compares three quantities: the fraction of pure duplicate edge pairs among direct failures, the full-range KS distance between the post-failure X X distributions of the two samples, and the miss/u of the Skellam rule on each sample. The difference in miss/u is judged by an equivalence test with bound ± 0.1 \pm 0.1 , with a one-sided level Bonferroni-corrected over the configurations in the same batch. The KS distance is compared with the asymptotic 95% critical value: 0.0075 with 65,000 failures on each side and 0.011 with 20,000 on the direct side. Because X X is discrete, this comparison is conservative. The control has two groups, and Figure H.2 summarizes both.

sections.heading: Low-load group.
sections.text: Most of the 105 planted configurations in the statistical experiments lie far from the critical load, so the expected number of duplicate edge pairs μ \mu (Appendix D ) is small, and Lemmas D.2 and D.3 make the failure probability of the same order as μ \mu . Direct sampling is infeasible for most of these configurations: among the 77 planted configurations with k = 4 , 5 k=4,5 , 76 have μ \mu below 10 − 6 10^{-6} , with a minimum of about 10 − 19 10^{-19} , and the feasibility pilot observes no failure in 68 of 75 configurations; collecting 65,000 failures requires at least 6.5 × 10 10 6.5\times 10^{10} trials, and about half the configurations require more than 10 15 10^{15} , beyond the feasible range of direct sampling. On the other hand, the distance between the planted distribution and the failure-conditioned distribution is controlled by Lemma D.2 , with an error term that tends to zero when d = o ⁡ ( M ) d=o(M) . The region where direct sampling is hardest is precisely where this approximation is most accurate. The low-load group selects the 12 configurations for which direct sampling remains affordable, covering c = 0.5 c=0.5 to 64 and load 0.04 to 0.71, with the number of direct trials fixed by μ \mu before sampling. Each planted side has 65,000 failures; the direct side has about 65,000 failures for k = 3 k=3 and for ( k , M , d ) = ( 4,256 , 16 ) (k,M,d)=(4,256,16) and ( 5,256,128 ) (5,256,128) , and about 20,000 for the other 6 configurations, where failures are rarer. Table H.1 gives the results, and the two samples agree on all 12 configurations. The fraction of pure duplicate edge pairs among direct failures ranges from 0.988 to 1.000, consistent with the mechanism in Lemma D.2 . At u = 0.05 u=0.05 , all 95% intervals of the difference contain zero; the equivalence test passes for all 4 configurations with k = 3 k=3 and for 5 of the 8 configurations with k = 4 , 5 k=4,5 , while the other 3 ( ( 4 , 1024 , 512 ) (4,1024,512) , ( 5,256 , 32 ) (5,256,32) , ( 5,256 , 64 ) (5,256,64) ) have only about 20,000 direct failures, with interval endpoints within ± 0.13 \pm 0.13 . At u = 0.01 u=0.01 , only ( 4 , 1024 , 512 ) (4,1024,512) has a difference interval excluding zero, equal to − 0.16 -0.16 (interval [ − 0.30 , − 0.02 ] [-0.30,-0.02] ), meaning higher miss in the planted sample. sections.heading: H.4 Random-sign encoding does not change decoding
sections.text: The decoding-equivalence test ( Exp-DEC ) compares first-round decoding under standard encoding and random-sign encoding. Across all paired trials, the two encodings agree on success and failure, the recovered results agree with the true residual core, and the decoder never falsely accepts a non-pure cell. The test uses the two-round protocol’s actual IBLT encoder and decoder, builds the two parties’ tables, and subtracts them. The test has three groups, each answering one question. The first group covers the full load range and all sign compositions, confirming equivalence over the whole parameter range with a large sample. The second group samples loads more densely near the peeling threshold, where the failure probability changes fastest with load and agreement is most sensitive; Table 6.1 of the main text also comes from this group. The third group examines the intermediate steps of decoding, counting rejected candidates and comparing how the checksum workload of the two encodings varies with sign composition. All three groups use the same construction and verification.

sections.heading: Construction and verification.
sections.text: Each trial regenerates distinct keys and fresh seeds for the cell hash, sign hash, and checksum hash; both encodings share the same keys and hashes. We first verify cell by cell that the three fields after cancellation of the common elements match those obtained by encoding the difference directly, then run decoding. An independent reference uses only the unsigned incidence graph of the true difference and computes its residual 2-core by the degree-one rule. Whenever the actual decoder accepts a key, we check the true residual degree, key, and direction, then update the reference state; these checks cover trajectories ending in both success and failure. After termination, we verify that the recovered keys are exactly the difference outside the 2-core, with all directions correct, reconstruct the three fields from the true residual, compare them cell by cell, and check that all fields are zero if and only if the residual core is empty.

sections.heading: First group: full load grid.
sections.text: The configurations use k ∈ { 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 10 } k\in\{3,4,5,6,10\} and M ∈ { 64 , 1024 , 16384 } M\in\{64,1024,16384\} . The load is d / ( α c ​ M ) ∈ { 0.5 , 0.95 , 1 , 1.05 , 3 } d/(\alpha_{c}M)\in\{0.5,0.95,1,1.05,3\} , and the positive-direction ratio d + / d d_{+}/d with target values 0 , 1 / 4 , 1 / 2 , 3 / 4 , 1 0,1/4,1/2,3/4,1 ; we round d d and d + d_{+} to integers from the target values. We use the corresponding peeling threshold for each k k , giving 375 configurations in total. The number of common elements is min ⁡ { 1000 , M } \min\{1000,M\} . For M = 64 , 1024 , 16384 M=64,1024,16384 , we run 3,000,000, 900,000, and 100,000 trials per configuration, respectively, for a total of 500,000,000 trials, with 100,000,000 for each k k . Table H.3 reports the results by k k . Across all configurations, we observe zero paired success/failure disagreements, non-pure acceptances, incorrect recoveries, or residual-core disagreements. The two decoders together check 211,516,840,988 acceptance operations, all satisfying the true degree-one and direction conditions.

sections.heading: Second group: near the threshold.
sections.text: The configurations use k ∈ { 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 10 } k\in\{3,4,5,6,10\} , M ∈ { 1024 , 16384 , 65536 } M\in\{1024,16384,65536\} , 10 load values between 0.90 and 1.05, and d − / d ∈ { 0 , 1 / 2 } d_{-}/d\in\{0,1/2\} . For M = 1024 , 16384 , 65536 M=1024,16384,65536 , we run 100,000, 20,000, and 10,000 trials per configuration, respectively, for a total of 13,000,000, and all checks pass. At M = 16384 M=16384 , the failure probability ranges from 0.020 to 0.060 at load 0.99 and from 0.993 to 0.998 at load 1.01; at M = 65536 M=65536 , almost no trials fail at load 0.99 and almost all fail at load 1.01. After failure, the decoder still recovers the difference outside the 2-core. At M = 65536 M=65536 and load 1.02, the average recovery fraction ranges from 0.18 ( k = 10 k=10 ) to 0.50 ( k = 3 k=3 ).

sections.heading: Third group: rejected candidates.
sections.text: Rejected candidates are cells with count ± 1 \pm 1 that fail the checksum or the cell-ownership check. Paired trials count them separately for each encoding. The configurations use M = 16384 M=16384 , k ∈ { 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 10 } k\in\{3,4,5,6,10\} , load 0.5 , 0.95 , 1 0.5,0.95,1 , and nine values of d − / d d_{-}/d from 0 to 1 in steps of 1 / 8 1/8 , with 50,000 trials per configuration for a total of 6,750,000, and all checks pass. Figure H.3 reports the results for k = 3 k=3 to 6. Standard encoding has no rejected candidates under one-sided differences because the count equals the degree; as the difference approaches balanced, more opposite-sign cancellation occurs and more candidates are rejected. Under random-sign encoding, the number of rejected candidates differs by at most 0.3% across the nine sign compositions and equals the standard value in the balanced case, consistent with Proposition 3.2 : the coding coefficient is an iid random sign independent of ( d + , d − ) (d_{+},d_{-}) . The results for k = 10 k=10 follow the same pattern, with both encodings yielding about 1.27 rejected candidates per difference key at load 1. Across the three groups, the two decoders together reject 2.8 × 10 11 2.8\times 10^{11} non-pure candidates with count ± 1 \pm 1 , with zero false acceptances; the cell-ownership check rejects zero candidates, and the checksum rejects every incorrect candidate. sections.heading: H.5 The post-failure estimate is conditionally unbiased for every sign composition
sections.text: Under random-sign encoding, the conditional mean of the post-failure X X agrees with zero on all tested configurations, whereas the conditional mean under standard encoding varies with sign composition and k k . We give the results for both encodings and then describe the data of Figure 6.1 in the main text.

sections.heading: Random-sign encoding.

sections.heading: H.7 Conditional miss rate and extra capacity at finite size
sections.text: This section supplements the numerical results of Section 6.4 . The main text concludes that the Skellam rule keeps the conditional miss rate near u u on all configurations, the Gaussian rule does so only for large c c , and the extra capacity ( U − d ) / d (U-d)/d of the two rules is almost the same and decreases as M − 1 / 2 M^{-1/2} . We first give the complete results of the statistical experiments ( Exp-STAT ), the miss/u and extra capacity of both rules, and then recheck the configurations closest to the risk bound with independent samples ( Exp-WORST ).

sections.heading: Conditional miss rate of the Skellam rule.
sections.text: Of the 189 configurations of the statistical experiments ( Exp-STAT ), 84 use direct sampling and 105 use planted sampling. Before judging whether miss/u exceeds 1, we consider sampling error: each configuration has about 20,000 failures, corresponding to about 200 misses at u = 0.01 u=0.01 , so the standard error of miss/u is about 0.07. At this precision, the Skellam rule’s maximum miss/u on direct-sampling configurations is 1.04 (the same at both levels of u u , occurring within the critical window), indistinguishable from 1; the maximum on planted configurations is 1.03, computed under the planted distribution. On direct-sampling configurations with c ≥ 8 c\geq 8 , the medians at the two levels of u u are 0.79–0.86 and 0.95–0.97. Low-load configurations with c < 8 c<8 are more conservative, with a median of at most 0.76 at u = 0.01 u=0.01 , because of the discrete structure: the lower tail is concentrated on a few lattice points and the rule cannot use the whole risk budget exactly. Under the Skellam rule every sample has at least one accepted candidate; if no candidate is accepted, U = + ∞ U=+\infty , which does not count as a miss.

sections.heading: Excess of the Gaussian rule.
sections.text: For c ≥ 8 c\geq 8 , the Gaussian rule’s miss/u is 0.83–1.19 across all configurations, at the same level as the Skellam rule. As c c decreases, the excess grows rapidly. Table H.7 lists the values at fixed c c for M = 16384 M=16384 , corresponding to the triangles with c ≤ 16 c\leq 16 in Figure 6.4 of the main text: at u = 0.01 u=0.01 it is about 8–11 at c = 1 c=1 and above 33 at c = 0.5 c=0.5 . Comparing table sizes, the values at M = 4096 M=4096 and 16384 differ by at most 10% for c ≤ 4 c\leq 4 , so the excess does not vanish as the table grows, consistent with the finite limit in Theorem 5.3 . For very small c c there is another case: when the observation lies near d − 2 d-2 , observations for d = 2 , 3 d=2,3 fall below the acceptance threshold of every candidate, the Gaussian rule returns + ∞ +\infty , and no miss occurs.

sections.heading: Worst-configuration test ( Exp-WORST ).
sections.text: The maximum miss/u of the statistical experiments lies within sampling error, but each configuration has only about 20,000 failures, which is insufficient to confirm that the highest-risk configurations also meet the target. This test uses samples independent of the statistical experiments ( Exp-STAT ) to recheck the Skellam rule’s conditional miss rate on the configurations closest to the risk bound, with both the selection rule and the sample sizes fixed before sampling. We first select the 5 configurations whose miss/u exceeds 1 in exploration; the remaining slots are filled in descending order of the larger of the two one-sided 95% exact upper bounds divided by u u in the statistical experiments ( Exp-STAT ). Four highly ranked configurations have only planted samples, because direct sampling cannot obtain failures at feasible cost, and the rule skips them in favor of later configurations; their miss/u under Q Q is at most 1.02. Only one of the selected 12 configurations uses M = 256 M=256 . The criteria are also fixed before sampling. The 12 configurations and two levels of u u give 24 judgments. A judgment passes if its one-sided simultaneous confidence upper bound is at most 1.1 ​ u 1.1u , using the Clopper–Pearson interval with a Bonferroni correction over the 24 judgments. Sample sizes are chosen by power: for each configuration and level of u u , we use the previously estimated 95% Wilson upper bound (at most 1) as the planning value, choose the failure count that gives a passing probability of at least 1 − 0.2 / 24 1-0.2/24 , and take the larger count over the two levels, so that at the planning value the probability that all 24 judgments pass is at least 80%. We sample in blocks and analyze all blocks through the first point at which the cumulative failure count in block order reaches the target; stopping depends only on the failure count. All 24 judgments pass, with a maximum upper bound of 1.024 ​ u 1.024u ; 22 of the 24 two-sided 95% intervals lie entirely below 1 and the other 2 cover 1. sections.heading: H.8 Reliability and communication cost of the two-round protocol
sections.text: The protocol experiments ( Exp-PROTO ) run the complete two-round synchronization on a real IBLT, corresponding to Section 6.5 of the main text. They test whether, when the second-round table length is set from the upper bound after a first-round failure, both the final reliability and the communication cost approach those of an oracle that knows the true d d .

sections.heading: Trial construction.
sections.text: Each trial generates common elements and difference elements separately, with all differences on the A A side for one-sided differences and half on each side for balanced differences. Common elements cancel in the difference table but participate as usual in table construction and cell-by-cell subtraction. The two rounds use independent cell hashes and share the sign hash and checksum hash. Trials that succeed in the first round require no upper bound, so only first-round-failure trials enter the comparison; the two levels of u u are evaluated separately on the same batch of trials. All upper bounds also share the same keys and hashes: for each first-round failure we record U b U_{b} , the second-round size, and the second-round outcome for each bound, so different bounds can be compared in paired fashion by trial. The second round decodes independently on the new table, consistent with Theorem 5.7 ; beyond the table length of Section 3.2 it imposes a minimum of 64 cells. All second-round recovery results match the true difference element by element.

sections.heading: Communication volume and sample size.
sections.text: We count 20 bytes per cell: 4 bytes for the transmitted count and 8 bytes each for keySum and checksum, plus an 8-byte global counter for random-sign encoding. Both levels of u u use the same number of trials per configuration, set to give about 20,000 first-round failures, ⌈ 2 × 10 4 / Pr ^ ​ ( F 1 ) ⌉ \lceil 2\times 10^{4}/\widehat{\Pr}(F_{1})\rceil , with a cap of 3,000,000; the 13 configurations with no first-round failure in the pilot receive a fixed 100,000 trials. Among them, the 8 configurations with k = 4 , 5 k=4,5 at load 0.95 and M 1 ≥ 4096 M_{1}\geq 4096 still have no first-round failure in these trials and contribute only to the failure-rate and byte statistics. Intervals for the success-rate difference use the Newcombe hybrid score method for paired proportion differences. Table H.9 summarizes the protocol results by M 1 M_{1} and u u . The final failure rate of both rules is at most 0.3% even at the smallest M 1 = 256 M_{1}=256 , and the conditional miss rate on balanced configurations agrees with the statistical experiments ( Exp-STAT ) of Section 6.4 . Even when the upper bound is sufficient ( U b ≥ d U_{b}\geq d ), second-round peeling itself can still fail, accounting for 0.06–0.08% at M 1 = 256 M_{1}=256 . The oracle’s upper bound equals d d , so by Eq. ( 5.10 ) of Theorem 5.7 its two-round failure comes only from the second term, the failure of second-round peeling with sufficient capacity. The oracle’s second-round table is therefore smaller than those of the two rules, and in paired comparisons by trial the Skellam rule’s success rate is up to 0.35 percentage points higher than the oracle’s on some M 1 = 256 M_{1}=256 configurations. The bounds of the two rules occasionally underestimate d d , and the second-round margin 1 / ( 0.8 ​ α c ) 1/(0.8\alpha_{c}) absorbs this slight underestimate (Section 5.5 ), so their final failure rates stay at the oracle’s level. sections.heading: H.9 Computation cost
sections.text: The computation-cost measurement ( Exp-COST ) covers three parts: table size, construction time, and protocol time for the Skellam rule’s lookup implementation; sizing time and Poisson-table memory for online computation; and the extra first-round decoding time of random-sign encoding.

sections.heading: Measurement and configurations.
sections.text: The host has dual Intel Xeon Silver 4410Y processors (nominal 2.0 GHz, 24 physical cores and 48 logical CPUs), runs Linux, and uses a single-threaded Go implementation pinned to one core. Timing uses two runs. Before the first, we pause the host’s task queue and wait for all tasks in the current batch to finish. We record that core’s frequency and system load every 10 seconds; the frequency remains at 2.001 GHz throughout the run. Figure H.4 and Table H.11 come from this run. In the second run, with the task queue idle, we repeat protocol timing with an added lookup branch. Table 6.2 comes from this run; its online and Gaussian protocol times differ from the first run by less than 3%. Protocol timing uses M 1 = 16384 M_{1}=16384 and 100,000 common elements, with the same 40 trials per configuration repeated 10 times and branch order rotated across repetitions. The second run includes lookup, online, Gaussian rule, oracle, and standard-encoding branches. First-round decoding time is counted per trial.

sections.heading: Table lookup.
sections.text: Following Appendix G.5 , we build 24 tables for M 1 = 1024 , 16384 M_{1}=1024,16384 , k = 3 , 4 , 5 k=3,4,5 , and u = 0.01 , 0.05 u=0.01,0.05 , with R R covered up to first-round loads of 1.5 and 3. Every U U is below 2 16 2^{16} , so each entry occupies 2 bytes. At M 1 = 16384 M_{1}=16384 , tables covering load up to 1.5 occupy 121–172 KB and take 5–7 s to construct on a single thread; those covering load up to 3 occupy 241–345 KB and take 20–25 s. At M 1 = 1024 M_{1}=1024 , the tables occupy 8–22 KB and take less than 0.6 s to construct. For every R R in each table, we compare the stored result with the online implementation used in the experiments. All 24 tables agree entry by entry. A separately measured lookup at a random index takes about 1 ns. For protocol timing, we build three additional tables with M 1 = 16384 M_{1}=16384 and u = 0.01 u=0.01 , covering first-round loads up to 4, and likewise verify them entry by entry. All first-round failure observations fall within these tables. In the protocol, each lookup-branch sizing takes 0.40–0.88 μ \mu s, compared with 0.75–1.33 μ \mu s for the Gaussian rule measured in the same way. Both include timing overhead. Total protocol time for the lookup branch differs from the Gaussian rule by less than 0.5%.

sections.heading: Online sizing time and memory.
sections.text: The Skellam rule computes the upper bound online when parameters vary across synchronizations or observations exceed the lookup table’s range. It uses one Poisson table per candidate n n , and whether these tables can be reused determines the sizing time, so the timing distinguishes cache conditions. Poisson tables are kept in a main-memory cache managed by the program. A cache entry corresponds to one value in the Poisson table of some candidate n n and stores its probability and cumulative probability as two double-precision numbers, 16 bytes in total; the capacity is 16,000,000 entries (about 256 MB). When the cache exceeds its limit, the program evicts tables in least-recently-used order until the occupancy plus the size of the incoming table is at most half the capacity, then inserts the new table. We time sizing under three cache conditions: cold starts each sizing with an empty cache; session has the same receiver perform consecutive synchronizations at fixed ( M , k ) (M,k) , each possibly involving one or two protocol rounds and each processing a new observation, with the cache retained between synchronizations; warm immediately recomputes the same observation once. For sizing timings, we use the first 200 failure records per configuration from the statistical experiments ( Exp-STAT ) at M = 16384 M=16384 , repeating each of the four modes, cold, session, warm, and Gaussian rule, 10 times, with their order rotated across repetitions. Appendix G.4 predicts that sizing cost is roughly proportional to λ d \lambda_{d} , that is, roughly c 2 c^{2} , and the measurements agree. Figure H.4 fixes M M , with load proportional to c c . Cold time grows roughly as load to the power 1.9, or c 1.9 c^{1.9} , from 0.06–0.12 ms at load about 0.08 ( c = 8 c=8 ) to 69–84 ms at load 3. Cache reuse reduces the time markedly: session is about one fifth of cold, and warm about one sixth to one seventh. At load 3, the Poisson tables requested cumulatively in session exceed the cache limit, the program evicts some old tables, and session rises to 41–55 ms. In the full protocol, peak session memory for Poisson tables is 49–86 MB at load 1.05, 128–174 MB at load 1.5, and reaches the 256 MB limit at load 3. Gaussian rule sizing takes only 0.06–0.29 μ \mu s. The exact Skellam CDF can also be replaced by a Gaussian approximation at large parameters: in the exploration phase, across the 33 configurations with Poisson mean above 200, the miss count is unchanged, and the fraction of samples whose U U changes is at most 1.8% in 32 of these configurations, and 10% in the other configuration with only 10 samples. All results in this paper use the exact rule. Figure H.4: Skellam rule time per sizing ( M = 16384 M=16384 , single thread, cache limit 16,000,000 entries). (a) cold; (b) session (solid) and warm (dashed).

sections.heading: Extra decoding cost of random-sign encoding.
sections.text: This cost arises in the pure-cell candidate check of first-round decoding. The decoder treats cells with count ± 1 \pm 1 as candidate pure cells and confirms them with the checksum. Under standard encoding with one-sided differences, all keys have the same sign, so a cell with count ± 1 \pm 1 necessarily contains exactly one key and every candidate passes; with both positive and negative differences, for example three keys with signs + 1 , + 1 , − 1 +1,+1,-1 in one cell also give count + 1 +1 , and the checksum rejects such candidates. Under random-sign encoding the key signs are iid, so the situation equals that of balanced differences regardless of sign composition. A separate run (30 trials per configuration, 3 repetitions) counted the candidates checked per recovered key: random-sign encoding checks 1.77 ( k = 3 k=3 ) and 2.53 ( k = 4 k=4 ); standard encoding checks 1.00 under one-sided differences and matches random-sign encoding under balanced differences. Table H.11 gives the ratio of first-round decoding times of the two encodings. Under balanced differences the two are almost the same. Under one-sided differences, the extra time of random-sign encoding comes from the additional candidate checks, and the ratio grows with load; at load 3 it is about 3.1, because standard encoding stops almost immediately under one-sided differences. At load 3 the absolute times of both are only 0.04–0.16 ms, less than 1% of total protocol time. text: Random-Sign IBLTs: Calibration-Free Self-Sizing After Decoding Failure Skip to main content Report GitHub Issue × Title: Content selection saved. Describe the issue below: Description: Why HTML? Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.41211v1 [cs.DS] 30 Oct 2026 Random-Sign IBLTs: Calibration-Free Self-Sizing After Decoding Failure Min Wu Email: wumin@hdu.edu.cn Abstract In a two-round set reconciliation protocol based on an Invertible Bloom Lookup Table (IBLT), the first round sends a fixed-capacity table. If an oversized difference causes decoding failure, the receiver must estimate a safe upper bound on the unknown difference size d d from the sum of squared counts in the difference table to size the second-round table adaptively. The standard IBLT uses each element’s set direction as its accumulation sign. This couples the hypergraph-overlap bias induced by failure selection with the sign composition of the two-sided difference. A one-sided difference amplifies the estimation bias through contributions of the same sign, forcing existing schemes to rely on extensive offline simulation calibration over a grid of configurations. We propose the random-sign IBLT . A pseudorandom sign independent of the position mapping decouples failure selection from sign composition while preserving the number and width of cell fields and the peeling recovery capability. We prove that the estimator is exactly unbiased on every fixed failed hypergraph. For large differences, we prove a Gaussian limit for the estimation error conditioned on failure and derive a closed-form Gaussian upper bound. For small differences, we characterize a discrete limit distribution dominated by duplicate edge pairs and construct a Skellam upper-bound rule whose conditional miss rate is asymptotically at most the target risk, uniformly over all d ≥ 2 d\geq 2 without offline calibration. Five hundred million paired trials and end-to-end experiments with the real protocol spanning several orders of magnitude in load show that the random-sign IBLT eliminates direction sensitivity. For small differences, the conditional miss rate of the Gaussian upper bound exceeds the target by more than a factor of 8, whereas the Skellam upper-bound rule keeps it at or below the target level within sampling error across all 189 load configurations. The total two-round communication cost approaches that of an oracle using the true difference size in the same protocol. 1 Introduction Many distributed systems require two network endpoints holding sets A A and B B to find their symmetric difference A ​ △ ​ B A\triangle B , the elements present on only one side. This problem is called set reconciliation. The Invertible Bloom Lookup Table (IBLT) [ 17 , 13 ] is the standard data structure for this task. Each side builds a table of M M cells and hashes each element into the count, keySum, and checksum fields of k k cells. The receiver then subtracts the tables cell by cell. Shared elements contribute identical values to the same cells and cancel exactly, leaving only the contributions of the d = | A ​ △ ​ B | d=|A\triangle B| differing elements. An element present only in A A has direction + 1 +1 , and an element present only in B B has direction − 1 -1 . When the difference size d d is small enough relative to the table size M M (the load d / M d/M is below the peeling threshold), the receiver repeatedly finds a pure cell containing a single differing element and recovers all differing elements through peeling. Once d d exceeds the table’s capacity, peeling stalls and decoding fails. An IBLT presents a basic tension: the table size M M must be fixed at construction, yet the difference size d d remains unknown until synchronization completes. In practice, d d for the same pair of nodes can vary by several orders of magnitude over time. During routine synchronization, the two sides are nearly identical and d d is small. After recovery from a network partition or a batch write, d d can grow sharply. Allocating a large table for the worst case wastes bandwidth in most routine synchronizations. Allocating a small table causes decoding failure when the difference is large. The two-round protocol [ 32 ] addresses this tension. The first round sends a small table of fixed size, allowing routine small differences to complete in one round. If an oversized difference causes decoding failure, the count array of the difference table still retains the superimposed contributions of all d d differing elements. The receiver estimates an upper bound U U on d d from the sum of squared counts in this table. The second round allocates sufficient capacity based on U U and completes synchronization. The key requirement is to control the underestimate risk conditioned on failure (the conditional miss rate). If U < d U<d (a miss), insufficient capacity puts the second-round table at risk of another failure. An overly conservative U U wastes second-round bandwidth. The method in [ 32 ] uses the count sum and the sum of squared counts in the first-round difference table to construct an unbiased estimator d ^ \widehat{d} and obtain an upper bound U U by inversion. Estimating d d after failure is difficult because decoding failure itself selects the sample, and this selection couples with the sign composition of the set difference (the ratio of differing elements from A A to those from B B ). When we estimate d d with this sum-of-squares method, each element’s own contribution is fixed. The estimation error comes entirely from cross terms between differing elements that fall into the same cell. The standard IBLT uses each element’s set-membership direction ( + 1 +1 or − 1 -1 ) as its accumulation sign in count. Two elements with the same direction add when they share a cell, increasing the sum of squares. Elements with opposite directions cancel. Peeling success depends on how the position mappings of differing elements to cells overlap. Conditioning on failure therefore changes the overlap distribution. Together, these effects produce systematic bias in the failure sample. For a one-sided difference, all differing elements come from the same side. This is common in one-way synchronization, for example when a replica lacks only data newly written to the primary. All cross terms then have the same sign, so the change in overlap induced by failure is amplified in the sum of squared counts, substantially biasing the estimate. In two-way synchronization where each side writes new data, the numbers of differing elements on the two sides are comparable. For this balanced difference, positive and negative cross terms largely cancel, leaving the post-failure mean estimate nearly unchanged. The bias magnitude varies continuously with the ratio of differing elements on the two sides, and its sign reverses with the number of hashes k k (Section 2 ). After decoding failure, the receiver does not know whether the difference comes from one side or both. The observed sum of squared counts therefore cannot reveal how much is due to the true d d and how much to the direction bias induced by failure selection. Thus, except in deep overload, the upper-bound rule for the standard IBLT in [ 32 ] relies in practice on offline simulation calibration for each configuration; its analytic bound is too conservative for small M M and may yield no usable quantile. Our core insight is that separating an element’s set direction from its accumulation sign removes the source of this coupling. We therefore propose the random-sign IBLT. The change is lightweight: the two sides share a random-sign hash independent of the position mapping, assigning each key a random + 1 +1 or − 1 -1 . On insertion, the element’s random sign multiplies its contributions to all three fields: count, keySum, and checksum. This modification supports both decoding and estimation. Shared elements receive the same random sign in both tables and still cancel exactly after subtraction. A cell containing one unrecovered differing element has count + 1 +1 or − 1 -1 . Multiplying keySum by count cancels the random sign exactly (since ( ± 1 ) 2 = 1 (\pm 1)^{2}=1 ) and recovers the original key. Computing the key’s random sign and comparing it with count then reveals whether the key belongs to set A A or B B . Under ideal purity, the random-sign IBLT therefore peels exactly the same elements as the standard IBLT at every step. The decoding threshold, failure probability, and number and byte width of cell fields remain unchanged. For estimation, each differing element’s coding coefficient in the difference table becomes an independent uniform random sign, whether the difference is one-sided or balanced. Peeling success depends only on which cells the elements select (the mapping), while cancellation of the estimation error depends on the random signs. These are independent. For every mapping selected by failure, the random signs remain independent and uniform, so their contributions cancel in expectation. Using random signs to cancel cross terms is a classical idea from the AMS sketch and CountSketch [ 1 , 7 ] . We implement it in a peelable data structure, enabling one table to support both difference recovery and difference-size estimation and allowing rigorous statistical analysis of the post-failure estimator. Main results and contributions. We prove that the random-sign IBLT preserves the standard IBLT’s decoding behavior under ideal purity and that the joint distribution of the difference-table statistic and the mapping is identical for all sign compositions. Section 3 presents the encoding and peeling algorithm that achieves this decoupling. We then prove that the estimator d ^ \widehat{d} is exactly unbiased on every fixed mapping, giving conditional mean d d after failure, and fully characterize the conditional distribution of the estimation error across all load scales (Sections 4 and 5 ). For large differences, we derive a Gaussian rule from the conditional Gaussian limit. For small differences, we characterize a discrete limit distribution and construct a Skellam rule whose conditional miss rate is asymptotically at most the target risk, uniformly over all difference sizes without offline simulation calibration. We also lift the known duplicate-pair mechanism to the distribution level: at low load, the failure-conditioned distribution is close in total variation to the planted distribution, which reduces the conditional analysis of rare failures to direct computation under the planted distribution and yields an efficient planted sampling method. The experiments (Section 6 ) verify that random-sign and standard encoding have identical decoding behavior. They show that the Skellam rule keeps the conditional miss rate at or below the target level within sampling error across all 189 configurations spanning several orders of magnitude in load, whereas the Gaussian rule exceeds the target by more than a factor of 8 for small differences. With this rule, the two-round protocol reliably completes synchronization at a total transmission cost close to that of an oracle using the true d d in the same protocol. Structure of the paper. Section 2 introduces the standard IBLT model and analyzes its post-failure estimation bias. Section 3 presents the random-sign IBLT and the two-round protocol. Section 4 proves exact unbiasedness given the mapping and derives the Gaussian rule for large differences. Section 5 derives the discrete limit distribution for small differences and the Skellam rule for all scales. Section 6 reports the experimental evaluation. Sections 7 and 8 discuss related work, rule selection, and computational cost. The appendix contains complete proofs and supplementary experiments. 2 Model and post-failure estimation bias We introduce the standard IBLT and the ideal peeling model, define the conditional miss rate required by the two-round protocol, characterize failure at low load, and explain how the standard IBLT’s post-failure bias depends on sign composition. Appendix A collects the notation used throughout the paper. 2.1 The standard IBLT and the ideal peeling model The two sides hold sets A A and B B and seek their symmetric difference A ​ △ ​ B A\triangle B , whose size d = | A ​ △ ​ B | d=|A\triangle B| is unknown in advance. The standard IBLT consists of M M cells, each with three fields: count, keySum, and checksum. To insert a key x x , the cell hash selects k k distinct cells from [ M ] [M] and adds 1 1 , x x , and chk ⁡ ( x ) \mathrm{chk}(x) to their respective fields. Each side builds a table, and the tables are subtracted cell by cell. Shared keys contribute identical values to the same cells in both tables, so their contributions cancel in all three fields. Only the contributions of the d d differing keys remain. A key present only in A A has direction s i = + 1 s_{i}=+1 , and a key present only in B B has direction s i = − 1 s_{i}=-1 . We denote the numbers of keys in the two directions by d + d_{+} and d − d_{-} . The ordered pair ( d + , d − ) (d_{+},d_{-}) is the sign composition , and b = d + − d − = | A | − | B | b=d_{+}-d_{-}=|A|-|B| is the difference between the set sizes. We use two extreme sign compositions throughout: a one-sided difference , where all differing keys come from one side ( | b | = d |b|=d ), and a balanced difference , where both sides have the same number of differing keys ( d + = d − d_{+}=d_{-} , b = 0 b=0 ). Both correspond to common synchronization scenarios. A one-sided difference arises in one-way synchronization when only one side inserts or deletes entries. A balanced difference arises in two-way synchronization when each side modifies a small number of entries and the insertions and deletions roughly cancel. Practical loads usually lie between these extremes, depending on how much each side changes. Decoding proceeds by peeling. We repeatedly find a pure cell containing one unrecovered differing key, recover the key by multiplying keySum by count, verify it with the checksum, and remove its contribution from all k k cells it selects. Removal may make other cells pure. Peeling continues until no pure cell remains. Under ideal purity, the decoder accepts a cell as pure exactly when it contains one unrecovered differing key. Cells with count ± 1 \pm 1 that contain multiple differing keys are rejected by the checksum. Under this assumption, peeling success depends entirely on the mapping of differing keys to cells. View the M M cells as vertices and the k k cells selected by each differing key as a hyperedge. The difference table then corresponds to a random k k -uniform hypergraph: the d d differing keys independently and uniformly choose k k -subsets S i ⊆ [ M ] S_{i}\subseteq[M] , with different keys allowed to choose the same subset. We denote the unsigned mapping with key labels by 𝒢 \mathcal{G} and the overlap between two edges by H i ​ j = | S i ∩ S j | H_{ij}=|S_{i}\cap S_{j}| , the number of cells shared by differing keys i i and j j . On 𝒢 \mathcal{G} , pure cells are exactly the unsigned degree-one vertices. Peeling repeatedly deletes edges incident to these vertices. The deletion order does not affect the terminal state, which is always the hypergraph’s 2-core. A nonempty 2-core causes decoding failure, denoted by event F F , with failure probability Pr ⁡ ( F ) \Pr(F) . Thus F F depends only on the unsigned mapping 𝒢 \mathcal{G} . When the load d / M d/M is below the critical value α c \alpha_{c} (about 0.818 0.818 for k = 3 k=3 and 0.772 0.772 for k = 4 k=4 [ 26 , 12 ] ), peeling succeeds with high probability. Rare failures arise from small cores such as duplicate edge pairs, and their probability decays polynomially in M M . In the critical window of width of order M − 1 / 2 M^{-1/2} around α c \alpha_{c} , the failure probability rises from near zero to near one [ 11 ] . Above α c \alpha_{c} , the failure probability tends to one. 2.2 The two-round protocol and the conditional miss rate Because the capacity M M must be fixed before d d is known, the two-round protocol [ 32 ] first sends a small table of fixed size M 1 M_{1} . For a small difference, peeling succeeds in the first round. After a first-round failure, the receiver obtains an upper bound U U on d d from the difference table’s count array and chooses the second-round size m ⁡ ( U ) m(U) based on U U . The second round re-encodes and decodes using a fresh, independent cell hash. Let C v C_{v} denote the count of cell v v in the difference table. Following [ 32 ] , we define the estimator d ^ \widehat{d} of d d using the count sum ∑ v C v \sum_{v}C_{v} and sum of squares ∑ v C v 2 \sum_{v}C_{v}^{2} saved before peeling begins: d ^ = 1 k ⁡ ( 1 − k / M ) ​ ( ∑ v C v 2 − 1 M ​ ( ∑ v C v ) 2 ) , \widehat{d}=\frac{1}{k(1-k/M)}\biggl(\sum_{v}C_{v}^{2}-\frac{1}{M}\Bigl(\sum_{v}C_{v}\Bigr)^{2}\biggr), (2.1) and denote its unconditional standard deviation scale by s ⁡ ( n ) s(n) : s ⁡ ( n ) = 2 ​ n ​ ( n − 1 ) M − 1 . s(n)=\sqrt{\frac{2n(n-1)}{M-1}}. (2.2) For the standard IBLT, d ^ \widehat{d} is exactly unbiased for d d and has variance s ​ ( d ) 2 s(d)^{2} for every sign composition. This expectation is unconditional: it averages over all runs, regardless of failure F F . If we evaluated the upper bound U U over all runs, adding a few standard deviations to d ^ \widehat{d} would control the underestimate probability. In the two-round protocol, a successful first round ends the protocol immediately, without computing U U . Only after decoding failure (event F F ) does the receiver compute U U to size the second-round table. If U < d U<d , the second-round capacity falls below the prescribed margin, risking another failure. We call the event U < d U<d a miss and its probability conditioned on first-round failure, Pr ⁡ ( U < d ∣ F ) \Pr(U<d\mid F) , the conditional miss rate . The sizing rule must therefore satisfy Pr ⁡ ( U < d ∣ F ) ≤ u , \Pr(U<d\mid F)\leq u, (2.3) where u u is the target risk. In deployment, we can choose 0.01 0.01 or 0.05 0.05 , corresponding to a 1 % or 5 % underestimate risk. The two-round protocol incurs a miss only when the first round fails and the upper bound underestimates d d . This event has joint miss rate Pr ⁡ ( F , U < d ) = Pr ⁡ ( F ) ​ Pr ⁡ ( U < d ∣ F ) \Pr(F,\,U<d)=\Pr(F)\Pr(U<d\mid F) . Controlling the conditional miss rate at u u bounds the joint miss rate by u ​ Pr ⁡ ( F ) u\Pr(F) , both in overload, where failure is almost certain, and at low load, where it is rare. For failure samples without a miss ( U ≥ d U\geq d ), the second-round table has sufficient capacity margin to decode with high probability. Section 5.5 gives the complete decomposition of the total two-round failure rate. 2.3 Failure at low load and the planted distribution Eq. ( 2.3 ) must hold at all loads. Low load requires separate treatment. When d d is much smaller than M M , the failure probability decays polynomially in M M . Failure is then rare, making the distribution conditioned on F F difficult to analyze directly and requiring many simulated mappings for each failure sample. The structure of failure in this region is simple. Two edges with the same mapping form a duplicate edge pair. A single edge cannot form a 2-core, and two edges form a 2-core exactly when they are a duplicate edge pair. When d = o ⁡ ( M ) d=o(M) , 2-cores with three or more edges are negligible relative to duplicate edge pairs. Failure is therefore approximately equivalent to the existence of a duplicate edge pair. Conditioning on F F is close to planting a duplicate edge pair in a random mapping. We thus define the planted distribution : choose a pair of keys uniformly, assign both the same uniformly random k k -subset, and let all remaining keys choose their mappings independently and uniformly. Proposition 2.1 (Failure is determined by duplicate edge pairs when d = o ⁡ ( M ) d=o(M) ) . Fix k ≥ 3 k\geq 3 and let 2 ≤ d = o ⁡ ( M ) 2\leq d=o(M) . The failure probability is asymptotically equal to the expected number of duplicate edge pairs: Pr ⁡ ( F ) ∼ ( d 2 ) / ( M k ) \Pr(F)\sim\binom{d}{2}/\binom{M}{k} . The total variation distance between the distribution of 𝒢 \mathcal{G} conditioned on F F and the planted distribution tends to zero. Goodrich and Mitzenmacher [ 17 ] identify duplicate edge pairs as the main source of IBLT failure. The finite-length analysis of Yugawa and Wadayama [ 34 ] likewise shows that stopping sets of size 2 dominate. Proposition 2.1 extends this observation to a total variation approximation of the entire mapping for all d = o ⁡ ( M ) d=o(M) . Lemma D.2 in Appendix D gives the quantitative error bound and proof. Proposition 2.1 supports both theory and experiments. It replaces conditioning on failure with the planted distribution, under which direct calculations are straightforward. The limit theorems in Sections 4 and 5 use this approximation to handle conditioning on failure when d = o ⁡ ( M ) d=o(M) . The risk decomposition in Section 5.5 also uses it to estimate the first-round failure probability. For experiments, it enables direct sampling from the planted distribution, where every sample yields a failure. Section 6.1 uses this planted sampling to evaluate low-load configurations beyond the reach of direct sampling and checks its finite-size accuracy where both methods are feasible. 2.4 Post-failure bias of the standard IBLT Controlling Eq. ( 2.3 ) is difficult because the failure event F F selects the mapping 𝒢 \mathcal{G} . This selection changes the distribution of the overlaps H i ​ j H_{ij} . At low load, failure samples mainly contain duplicate edge pairs (Proposition 2.1 ), whose overlap is k k , increasing the conditional mean of H i ​ j H_{ij} . In the critical window and at higher load, failure corresponds to mappings with large cores. Such a core is a local structure, and the direction of the change in the conditional mean of H i ​ j H_{ij} depends on k k , as measured by c F c_{F} below. Statistics that depend on H i ​ j H_{ij} therefore require separate analysis after conditioning on F F . In the standard IBLT, the difference-table count is C v = ∑ i : v ∈ S i s i C_{v}=\sum_{i:v\in S_{i}}s_{i} , and each differing key’s coding coefficient is its fixed set direction s i ∈ { + 1 , − 1 } s_{i}\in\{+1,-1\} . In the sum of C v 2 C_{v}^{2} , the diagonal terms contribute exactly k ​ d kd . The estimation error comes entirely from the cross terms s i ​ s j ​ H i ​ j s_{i}s_{j}H_{ij} between keys sharing cells. Excess overlap raises d ^ \widehat{d} for same-sign pairs and lowers d ^ \widehat{d} for opposite-sign pairs. The conditional relative bias of d ^ \widehat{d} thus factors exactly into two terms. Proposition 2.2 (Bias decomposition of the standard IBLT) . In the standard IBLT, for any sign composition ( d + , d − ) (d_{+},d_{-}) , 𝔼 ⁡ [ d ^ ∣ F ] d − 1 = c F ​ ( b 2 d − 1 ) , c F = 𝔼 ⁡ [ H 12 ∣ F ] − k 2 / M k ⁡ ( 1 − k / M ) . \frac{\mathbb{E}[\widehat{d}\mid F]}{d}-1=c_{F}\Bigl(\frac{b^{2}}{d}-1\Bigr),\qquad c_{F}=\frac{\mathbb{E}[H_{12}\mid F]-k^{2}/M}{k(1-k/M)}. (2.4) The proof is in Appendix B . Since F F is invariant under permutations of key labels, 𝔼 ⁡ [ H i ​ j ∣ F ] \mathbb{E}[H_{ij}\mid F] is identical for all i ≠ j i\neq j . The formula uses differing keys 1 1 and 2 2 as a representative pair. The factor c F c_{F} depends only on failure selection of the mapping and measures the excess of inter-edge overlap in the failure sample over its unconditional mean k 2 / M k^{2}/M . The factor b 2 / d − 1 b^{2}/d-1 depends only on the sign composition ( d + , d − ) (d_{+},d_{-}) . For a one-sided difference ( | b | = d |b|=d ), every intersecting edge pair has sign product + 1 +1 , so b 2 / d − 1 = d − 1 b^{2}/d-1=d-1 . All excess overlap contributes with the same sign, fully amplifying its effect on d ^ \widehat{d} . For a balanced difference ( b = 0 b=0 ), there are d / 2 d/2 fewer same-sign pairs than opposite-sign pairs, giving a relative bias of − c F -c_{F} , whose magnitude is 1 / ( d − 1 ) 1/(d-1) of the one-sided value. Figure 2.1: Post-failure relative bias of the standard IBLT versus ( b / d ) 2 (b/d)^{2} ( M = 16384 M=16384 ). (a) k = 3 k=3 . (b) k = 6 k=6 . Each color denotes a failure probability. All configurations lie in the critical window: d / M d/M is 0.812–0.822 for k = 3 k=3 and 0.633–0.639 for k = 6 k=6 . Points are measurements, and lines follow Eq. ( 2.4 ). Figure 2.1 shows this decomposition at M = 16384 M=16384 for five failure probabilities (0.10 to 0.90) each for k = 3 k=3 and k = 6 k=6 . Within each configuration, all five sign compositions share the same batch of mappings and therefore identical peeling outcomes. Since b 2 / d − 1 = d ​ ( b / d ) 2 − 1 b^{2}/d-1=d(b/d)^{2}-1 , the relative bias at each failure probability is linear in ( b / d ) 2 (b/d)^{2} , with slope determined by c F c_{F} . We determine c F c_{F} from the one-sided point. The remaining predictions of Eq. ( 2.4 ) differ from the measurements by at most twice the standard error of the difference. For k = 3 k=3 at failure probability 0.10, the one-sided relative bias is + 0.70 % +0.70\% , corresponding to a bias of about 0.64 standard deviations s ⁡ ( d ) s(d) .
